Clinical trials Employees Professionals Media inquiries Financial assistance Contact us News & stories Help me find Doctors Specialties Locations Schedule My Health Connection Log in UCHealth Today All Innovative care Healthy living Stories News Live Colorado Español UCHealth Today > Measles and infants: How parents can protect babies from this highly contagious disease As measles infections rise in Colorado and the U.S., experts explain why infants are vulnerable and how families can protect newborns and young children. By: Joanna Bean Yesterday Infants are among the most vulnerable to measles because they are not routinely vaccinated until 12 months of age. Photo: Getty Images. Amid an increase in measles infections in the U.S., including a northern Colorado infant who contracted the highly infectious illness while the family traveled abroad, parents may have questions about how to keep their babies safe. Infants are among the most vulnerable to measles because they are not routinely vaccinated until 12 months of age. That means their protection against measles depends heavily on the immunity of people around them. In the early 2000s, U.S. health officials declared measles eradicated. But measles cases are on the rise in Colorado and elsewhere after declining vaccination rates. That, along with the annual winter season of cold, flu, RSV and other illnesses, means babies are particularly at risk of getting sick. To answer parents’ questions about keeping newborns and babies safe from measles and other wintertime illnesses, we consulted with two UCHealth doctors: Dr. Megan Ross, a pediatrician with UCHealth Estes Valley Medical Center, and Dr. Michael Ramos, a family medicine doctor with UCHealth Family Medicine – Parkview Pueblo West. Here’s what they recommend to keep newborns healthy and what families should do if they suspect they may have been exposed to measles or another illness and need medical care. What is measles, and why are cases rising in Colorado and the U.S.? Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world, Ross said. Infected people typically get sick with symptoms similar to those of a cold or the flu, namely fever, runny nose and red eyes. Then, a rash appears on the top of the body and moves downward. Symptoms typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure, and it can take up to 21 days for an infected person to get sick. How can parents prevent measles in newborns and older babies? Parents should vaccinate their babies to prevent measles once the baby turns a year old. Infants can get the measles vaccine as young as age six months if babies and their parents will be traveling to areas with measles outbreaks. Babies under the age of six months can’t get measles vaccines, so family members should protect babies from illnesses by staying up to date on their vaccines. Mothers can pass immunity to measles and other illnesses through their breast milk. Extended breastfeeding can help protect babies from getting sick. Sick people should stay away from newborns. Parents should make sure all visitors wash their hands carefully before visiting newborns. Do not allow visitors to kiss their baby on the head or face. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases on Earth, and nine of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed to measles will get it. Babies and older people who get measles can get very sick and can die from measles infections, and people who get measles also can suffer long-term health problems. Infected people can spread measles without knowing it because they can be contagious before having any symptoms. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the area. Measles is especially dangerous because it spreads so easily. Researchers have found that nine of 10 people who are not vaccinated and get exposed to the measles virus will get infected. “The outbreaks are so difficult to get a handle on because not everybody who is contagious has that stereotypical high fever and the rash,” Ross said. “They can look and feel totally fine, and those virus particles that they breathe out can hang in the air for two hours. Anybody nearby who isn’t vaccinated and protected against measles is then at risk for contracting measles.” That’s why so-called herd immunity is so important, Ross said. Herd immunity refers to having a high enough percentage of people vaccinated to prevent sustained transmission of measles. Herd immunity of 95% is required to stop a measles outbreak. But herd immunity for measles has waned in recent years as fewer children have received the vaccine, in part because of false information about vaccines that have left communities vulnerable to outbreaks. In Colorado, 90.9% of people ages one to 18 have received at least one dose of the MMR vaccine, which provides combined protection for measles, mumps and rubella, according to medical experts at the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. How measles creates immune amnesia in your body. The number of measles cases across the U.S. this year has surged to more than double the number of cases in 2025. As of Nov. 6, health officials at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed 5,182 measles cases across the country so far in 2026. That’s more than double the 2,289 confirmed in 2025. And at least two babies under age one have died from measles this year, with one confirmed death of an infant in Pennsylvania and another in Wisconsin. In Colorado, health officials confirmed 27 measles cases so far in 2026, compared to 36 cases in all of 2025. The Colorado cases include an infant in Weld County who contracted measles. The baby’s family sought care at multiple locations in the area in late October. Why is measles dangerous for infants and babies? Newborns and older people face higher risks of complications from measles if they contract it, Ross said. “When measles affects a kiddo, it makes them very sick,” she said. “They have a one in five chance of needing to be admitted to the hospital.” Complications of measles for babies include developing ear infections, viral pneumonia and encephalitis, or inflammation of the brain, which can cause seizures, loss of hearing and permanent brain damage. Parents should check with their medical provider as soon as possible any time a newborn has a fever. Mothers who are breastfeeding their babies can pass immunities that can prevent measles and other illnesses like the flu and colds to their babies through their milk. What should I do if I think my baby has been exposed to measles? Ross recommends parents call or send a message to their pediatrician or healthcare provider if they think their baby has been exposed to measles. Together, they can determine if the baby has symptoms and needs treatment. How do doctors treat measles in babies and children? Vitamin A will not kill the virus nor cure the complications, but it can help with a child’s recovery, especially for children who are deficient in Vitamin A. Ross encourages parents to feel empowered to remind family and friends that their baby’s immune system isn’t as strong as an older child’s, and to visit only if they’re healthy. “Anybody with any kind of illness should be masked or wait until feeling better before seeing a newborn,” she said. “For little ones, I would be very protective of who sees them.” Ramos encourages parents to practice good hand-washing hygiene to avoid passing along illness to their baby. news.content_title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status, Data Suggests
news.content: Supported by The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status, Data Suggests An international panel of scientific experts will convene on Tuesday to evaluate the status, but genetic data already shows the virus is once again entrenched in the United States. Measles is once again endemic — a constant and predictable presence — in the United States, 26 years after it was declared eliminated in the country, an analysis of genetic data from outbreaks of the disease has found. Data from the outbreaks will be the focus of deliberations by an international panel of scientific experts convening on Tuesday to decide whether the United States should lose its official designation as a nation that has eliminated measles. An announcement of the decision is expected on Nov. 17. The New York Times asked several scientists to analyze the publicly available genetic data before the meeting. Achieving elimination status in 2000 was a hard-fought public health victory for the United States. But with skepticism about the safety of vaccines growing in recent years, outbreaks have become more frequent. Over the past two years, cases have soared, with nearly 5,200 reported so far this year. Last week alone, Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin each reported a death associated with measles, bringing this year’s total to eight, more than the combined deaths from 2000 through 2024. To officially lose elimination status, a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a branch of the World Health Organization, must determine that the country has had uninterrupted transmission of measles for more than 12 months. Publicly available data shows that several chains of transmission have continued for more than a year in the United States, according to scientists who analyzed the data at the request of The New York Times. Three chains that were continuing in July 2026 — two in Utah and one in Arizona — can all be traced to an outbreak in Texas more than a year earlier. One of those, which was still continuing in Utah in September, had been circulating for over a year in that state, occasionally spilling over into Oregon and Washington. “This alone is strong evidence that there has been ongoing transmission for over a year,” said Bill Hanage, a co-director of the Center for Communicable Disease Dynamics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Another transmission chain detected in Virginia at the start of the year was still spreading in Iowa, Indiana and Pennsylvania as of mid-October. (There is often a delay of several weeks before genetic data is available online.) “There’s a general pattern of outbreaks seeding other outbreaks,” said J.T. McCrone, an evolutionary biologist at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center who helps oversee Nextstrain, the publicly available database that contains genetic information for measles and many other pathogens. “Measles is very contagious; it spreads very easily,” Dr. McCrone said. “We have a lot of connected communities in the U.S., and so you can hop from population to population and maintain a transmission chain.” Some critics consider the potential loss of elimination status a referendum on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for decades questioned the safety of vaccines in general and the measles vaccine in particular. He has falsely said that the measles vaccine can be fatal, that it contains fetal debris and that its effectiveness plummets over time. None of the eight Americans who died from measles this year had been vaccinated against the disease. (Four were infants who were too young for the shot.) Mr. Kennedy has repeatedly noted that measles is on the rise in many countries beyond the United States. Due in large part to a rise in vaccine hesitancy and misinformation since the pandemic, seven countries, including Canada, Spain and Britain, have lost their elimination status in the past two years. Mexico is expected to lose it this month along with the United States. But the explosion of cases in the United States has coincided precisely with his time in office. Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recorded nearly 2,300 cases and three deaths. Most cases of measles in the years since elimination were linked to travel abroad, particularly in countries where the disease is still endemic. But those importations did not spread widely and died out quickly because more than 95 percent of children in the United States had been immunized against the disease. That percentage dropped to 92.4 percent in the school year beginning in 2025, leaving nearly 300,000 kindergartners at risk. Rising vaccine hesitancy has led to sharp increases in parents seeking exemptions for their children from school vaccination requirements. The Covid pandemic exacerbated the problem, first by derailing routine immunizations and then by intensifying mistrust of vaccines. Mr. Kennedy’s statements from his pulpit as the country’s top health official also fueled misplaced fears that childhood vaccines might be more dangerous than the diseases they are intended to prevent. Regaining elimination status will require more than ending the current transmission chains, experts said. Public health officials will need to increase immunization rates across the country and cut down on the number of pockets into which the virus can jump. The measles virus evolves slowly, allowing the vaccine to be effective even without frequent updates. But its slow evolution also means that pinpointing how the virus is changing or moving requires deeper analyses. Scientists have typically relied on snippets of the measles virus, which was enough to identify the sporadic cases in the country. But they now have the technology to decode the full genetic sequences of the samples, giving them clearer insight into how the virus is changing and moving, and enabling them to distinguish endemic circulation from travel-associated cases. “If this outbreak had occurred in 2006, we wouldn’t have the technology to be able to do this,” said Robert Potter, a clinical microbiologist at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “We never really had to study measles from a genomic perspective before because there was no measles to sequence,” he added. “It’s giving us a lot of new information, but it’s information that we didn’t necessarily need to have.” Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them. news.content: Skip to main content News Economy Elections Environment Health Investigations Josh Shapiro Justice System Local Government Penn State Restaurant Inspections Rural Issues State Capitol More Topics Archives Bureaus State College Berks County Newsletters PA Post Good Day, Berks Talk of the Town PA Local The Investigator Access Harrisburg Games Crossword Mini Crossword News Quiz Slide Sudoku Word Flower Word Search WordroW About Our Mission Meet the Team Board of Directors Spotlight PA Partners Impact Events Careers Mobile Apps Contact Send a Tip Advertise With Us Donate Ways to Give Manage Your Membership How We're Funded Leaders in Action Spotlight PA Store Agentic Giving Menu Menu Newsletters Donate Search Journalism that Gets Results SM Investigations State College Berks County About Main content Health The US and Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here’s what to know by Mike Stobbe of the Associated Press | Nov. 13, 2026 Marco Ugarte / Associated Press Share: NEW YORK (AP) — International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths. Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations’ borders. “It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backward,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments. Here’s a look at the meeting’s deliberations and why they are important. International health experts are poring over measles data this week In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024. “It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have eliminated measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998. The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said. The CDC says loss of measles elimination status won’t change its approach A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement. But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation’s health agencies. Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and laud Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say. The US is having its worst measles year in decades Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak. But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities. Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991. At least 50 people have died from measles in Mexico A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016. Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected. As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old. The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom and Uzbekistan lost their status. ___ Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. Here’s what to know by Mike Stobbe of the Associated Press | Nov. 13, 2026 Marco Ugarte / Associated Press Share: NEW YORK (AP) — International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths. Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations’ borders. “It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backward,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments. Here’s a look at the meeting’s deliberations and why they are important. International health experts are poring over measles data this week In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024. “It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have eliminated measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998. The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said. The CDC says loss of measles elimination status won’t change its approach A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement. But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation’s health agencies. Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and laud Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say. The US is having its worst measles year in decades Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak. But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities. Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991. At least 50 people have died from measles in Mexico A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016. Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected. As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old. The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom and Uzbekistan lost their status. ___ Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. news.content_title: Wisconsin reports 2nd measles death as outbreak reaches 649 cases
news.content: Wisconsin reports 2nd measles death as outbreak reaches 649 cases By WDIO Measles Vaccine (MMR). (CBS Evening News) In Brief Wisconsin reports a second child death linked to the ongoing 2026 measles outbreak, with 649 cases across 20 counties since August. Health officials are urging vaccination, with over 45,600 MMR doses given and nearly 2,000 more delivered to affected communities. Residents are advised to check vaccination records, stay home if exposed, and contact health care providers if symptoms develop. A second child has died from measles in Wisconsin as the outbreak continues, according to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) and the Grant County Health Department. To protect the privacy of the family and child, no further details about the death will be released. RELATED: Wisconsin’s first death of measles reported since 1990 Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air and close contact. It can cause life-threatening complications, especially for children under 5, pregnant people and those with weakened immune systems. As of November 13, 2026, there have been 649 measles cases in 20 counties since August, the highest number in Wisconsin in more than 35 years. DHS noted that actual case numbers may be higher, as not everyone seeks medical care or gets tested. RELATED: Measles cases in Minnesota hit highest total in 36 years DHS response and vaccination efforts DHS continues to work with local and Tribal health departments and health care partners to coordinate statewide response efforts. These include case tracking, information sharing, testing and vaccination. Since August 1, 2026, nearly 2,000 doses of MMR vaccine have been delivered to communities with confirmed cases, and over 45,600 total doses have been administered by local agencies and health care providers. DHS has also provided support to prevent wider spread in communities and health care settings. Prevention and public health advice “Preventing the spread of measles takes action from all of us,” said State Health Officer and Division of Public Health Administrator Paula Tran. “From making sure our families are protected by getting the recommended vaccinations to staying home when we may have been exposed, we encourage everyone to work together to protect those who are most vulnerable to serious illness. Stay informed, look out for one another, and take the actions you can to help stop the spread of measles and keep our communities healthy and safe.” DHS urges everyone to be proactive by getting the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, which is about 97% effective with two doses. Wisconsin residents can check their vaccination records online using the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or by contacting their health care provider or local health department. If exposed to measles, DHS advises people to stay home. Anyone who develops a fever and rash, especially if unvaccinated or exposed, should contact their health care provider and call ahead before visiting a clinic or hospital. For more information about measles in Wisconsin, including vaccination recommendations and current case activity, residents can visit the DHS measles webpage

OffOn Stream on Measles cases nationwide top 5,400 as deaths rise to 10 Wisconsin and Pennsylvania reported additional measles deaths Friday. ByYouri Benadjaoud November 13, 2026, 3:42 PM Share New measles deaths were reported in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania on Friday, bringing the total number of measles deaths in the United States to 10. Measles cases nationwide have topped 5,400, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported earlier. The CDC says 5,412 infections have been reported across 45 states. That is 230 more infections since the update last Friday. Between 2000 to 2024, the U.S. averaged 180 cases annually. Wisconsin health officials on Friday reported a second measles death in the state, as Pennsylvania health officials also reported an additional death. The nationwide total for measles deaths is now at 10 -- seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. A decision about the U.S. measles elimination status could come as soon as Friday. A measles, mumps and rubella virus vaccine at Union Community Care clinic in Lancaster, Pa., Oct. 8, 2026. Jessie Wardarski/AP Photo Vaccination rates The number of kindergartners vaccinated with the measles vaccine dropped from 95% in 2019 to 92% in 2026. Herd immunity is typically provided at 95% vaccination rates in communities. There are now roughly 300,000 kindergartners that entered classrooms this year without being vaccinated. Related What parents need to know as measles outbreaks spread across the US The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine comes in two doses. The first dose is received between 12-15 months of age, followed by a second dose between 4-6 years of age. Those two doses are 97% effective at preventing infection. Even if still infected, those vaccinated are less likely to become severely ill. More on measles Measles in the most contagious disease in the world. A sick individual can infect 90% of unvaccinated people they come into contact with. The virus lives on surfaces and in the air two hours after a sick person leaves the room. Signs point the way to measles testing in the parking lot of the Seminole Hospital District across from Wigwam Stadium on February 27, 2025 in Seminole, Texas. Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images, FILE Measles is not just a rash. One in 10 children with measles get ear infections and one in 10 children with measles get diarrhea. One in 5 people that are unvaccinated land in the hospital, while one in 20 children get pneumonia. Nearly one to three of every 1,000 children who become infected die from respiratory and neurological complications. analysis.brief_en: The United States has reported a total of 5,412 measles cases across 45 states, with 10 deaths. This marks a significant increase from the previous update, with 230 new cases reported. Vaccination rates among kindergartners have dropped to 92%, below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity. The measles virus, highly contagious and potentially fatal, has infected 300,000 unvaccinated kindergartners, with severe complications including ear infections, diarrhea, and pneumonia. Health officials are investigating and implementing prevention measures, with a decision on the U.S. measles elimination status expected soon.

Photograph: Juan Diego Reyes for The Washington Post via Getty Images CDC reports six measles deaths in 2026 as US battles worst outbreak in 35 years Figures highlight spread of virus, officially declared eliminated in US in 2000, but CDC does not identify which states accounted for deaths The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported six measles-related deaths in the US this year, according to figures published on its website on Thursday, as the country faces its most severe resurgence of the disease in decades. The newly reported total is twice the number of deaths recorded in 2025, highlighting the spread of the highly infectious virus, which was officially declared eliminated in the US in 2000. The country is currently experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991. More than 5,400 cases reported nationwide, according to data from the Johns Hopkins University International Vaccine Access Center tracker. Pennsylvania has been the state most severely affected by the outbreak, with officials confirming six measles-associated deaths in the state this year. A child also died in New York on election day, followed days later by the death of an infant in Wisconsin. Active outbreaks have been reported in nearly every US state. The Wisconsin department of health services confirmed the infant’s death, while New York recorded its first known measles-related fatality in more than three decades. The CDC did not identify which states accounted for the six deaths included in its official count. The difference in the reported figures followed a change in how the CDC, operating under US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, tracks measles fatalities. The CDC is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time, according to a note published to the agency’s website on 4 September. Kennedy previously argued without evidence that two of the deaths in Pennsylvania may not be from measles. He asked Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, not to count the deaths in the official CDC tally, according to reporting by Reuters. The day after the Reuters report was published, the CDC changed its data source on measles deaths. Measles is preventable through the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which offers approximately 97% protection after two doses. The US could lose its measles elimination status this week, a development likely to further define Kennedy ’s legacy of interference in vaccine policies. Losing that designation would place the US alongside Canada and several countries in Europe and Asia where measles had previously been eliminated before making a comeback. news.content_title: With measles surging, the US is likely to lose 'elimination' status. Vaccines offer best hope
news.content: With measles surging, the US is likely to lose 'elimination' status. Vaccines offer best hope Advertisement Updated: 12:14 PM MST Nov 13, 2026 Editorial Standards i By Madison Czopek, PolitiFact's Well Informed With measles surging, the US is likely to lose 'elimination' status. Vaccines offer best hope Updated: 12:14 PM MST Nov 13, 2026 Editorial Standards i By Madison Czopek, PolitiFact's Well Informed Babies are dying in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and New York. A high school closed in Pennsylvania. A Texas labor and delivery unit had to enact emergency protocols after measles was detected in a laboring mother. This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed . Advertisement Measles is spreading in the U.S. at a pace not seen in over three decades. The highly contagious respiratory disease can cause a rash, cough, runny nose, fever, watery eyes and high fevers. It can lead to hospitalization and death. With communities nationwide feeling the disease’s effects, the U.S. is on track to lose the sought-after "measles elimination" status it achieved 26 years ago. The Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that coordinates public health efforts across dozens of countries, designates nations as having achieved measles elimination when robust surveillance shows they have ended " endemic " — or regular and sustained — virus transmission. Elimination status means a country has not seen very large measles outbreaks and has not had uncontrolled domestic virus transmission for a year or more. This is no longer true of the United States, data shows . Pennsylvania measles cases reach more than 1,000. Track outbreaks in your state Measles cases skyrocketed in 2025 and 2026. This year alone, the country has already recorded more than 5,100 measles cases — the highest number seen in 35 years. With case counts rising each week, experts say there’s only one way to end the spread: increased measles vaccination. Any community with vaccine coverage below 95% is particularly vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles is "exquisitely contagious," said Jennifer Nuzzo, a Brown University epidemiology professor who tracks measles . "The virus just has to show up, and then it explodes." How many measles cases have U.S. health authorities recorded this year? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had reported 5,182 measles cases and six deaths in 2026 as of Nov. 6. The CDC says it counts only confirmed cases . Other public health data aggregators have recorded higher case counts. Johns Hopkins’ U.S. Measles Tracker reported 5,400 cases in 2026 as of Nov. 11. That total reflects lab-confirmed measles cases compiled from state and county health departments, county-level news releases and news articles. Wisconsin infant dies amid measles outbreak, the third measles-related death this week in the US Brown University School of Public Health’s Tracking Report newsletter tallied 5,478 cases and nine deaths as of Nov. 5 — eight confirmed by states and one confirmed by a local coroner. Its report pulls data from state health department websites and counts cases by the dates they were reported to health organizations. Other organizations often mark the cases by the date the measles rash is detected. How many measles outbreaks have been documented this year? With two months left in the year, the CDC reports 43 new measles outbreaks in 2026, defining “outbreak” as three or more related cases. The agency reported 48 outbreaks total last year and 16 in 2024. The U.S. has recorded more than 100 new measles cases each week for 13 weeks straight . How many states are seeing large measles outbreaks? So far in 2026, 13 states have seen more than 100 measles cases, according to CDC data. In 2025, just five states surpassed 100 cases. At least six states are currently battling sizable measles outbreaks. Pennsylvania’s outbreak is the largest this year by far among all states, with officials documenting more than 1,500 cases and six measles-associated deaths, according to state health department data as of Nov. 9. Hundreds more cases have been documented in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin. Not everyone infected with measles seeks medical care, so these figures are likely undercounts . And states often record a measles-associated death if the person died while having measles. Grandparents urged to get measles, flu, and other shots before meeting a newborn in the U.S. Under the second Trump administration, the CDC has not recorded the same number of U.S. measles deaths as states, after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an antivaccine activist, publicly questioned whether evidence sufficiently demonstrated measles was the cause of death. In the U.S., officials typically expect about one to two deaths per 1,000 measles cases. Given the nine measles-associated deaths states have reported this year, "there is reason to believe that we are far, far from totally enumerating the amount of infections," Nuzzo said. Why is the U.S. likely to lose its measles elimination status? The Pan American Health Organization commission that assesses measles and rubella elimination in the Americas was meeting Nov. 10-13 and expects to release its decision about the U.S. status on Nov. 17 . Many public health experts believe measles is once again endemic in the U.S. In early 2026, Maimuna Majumder, a computational epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital, and other researchers analyzed the country’s measles data. Since then, Majumder said it “seems inevitable” that the U.S. would lose its elimination status. The U.S. is currently seeing uncontrolled measles spread that has lasted for more than 12 months, and available evidence signals that the actual number of infections surpasses the recorded case totals, Nuzzo said. "By every measure that matters, measles is no longer a rare condition in the United States," Nuzzo said. "It has returned to continual spread — spread that doesn’t require imported infections." 'We are deeply saddened': New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years Dr. Jonathan Temte, a University of Wisconsin public health and community engagement professor emeritus, said losing this designation — one the United States helped define years ago — says a lot about how the country’s public health and medical systems are doing. Measles elimination is a goal countries work toward, Nuzzo said: "It is a point of pride when you achieve it, and it is a point of embarrassment when you lose it." Could the U.S. eliminate measles again? Yes. Doing so starts with containing outbreaks. Canada lost its measles elimination designation in 2025, but still managed to control measles spread in 2026 — declaring its multi-jurisdictional measles outbreak over in October. Brazil lost its elimination status in 2019 and regained it in 2024. The U.S. was largely holding steady low case numbers from 2000 until 2019, when it recorded 1,274 cases. The 2018-19 outbreak was centered in New York City and surrounding counties, and officials responded by declaring a public health emergency, mandating vaccinations, closing schools with measles transmission, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school and doing public outreach, KFF reported . The New York outbreak was interrupted by August 2019 — less than 12 months after it began. It's important that sick people stay home and unvaccinated people who’ve been exposed undergo a 21-day quarantine , but widespread transmission only ends with increased vaccination, Nuzzo said. 'Measles-associated deaths': Dissecting the dispute between RFK Jr. and Pennsylvania's governor Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina, presented the country’s measles report to the Pan American Health Organization commission. Vaccination is key, he said. "If we do not want an incurable and deadly disease to stalk our kids in schools, playgrounds and churches," Brewer said, adding, "We need to get more kids vaccinated." It's uncertain how public health officials will respond should the U.S. lose its status. In a Tuesday interview with Reuters , CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said she didn’t foresee the federal government altering its approach. "We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states," she said. PolitiFact Staff Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed . It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television. Event Date: Nov 5, 2026 During a special post-election discussion and live podcast taping, KFF experts and journalists provided analysis and insights about what the election results could mean for health policy and take audience questions. Part of the discussion focused on public opinion survey data on how voters weighed health care as they went to the polls nationally and in the four states with abortion-related ballot initiatives. Watch the full discussion KFF Election Poll Analysis: What the Midterms Mean for Health Care KFF’s two new interactive dashboards examine how voters weighed key health care issues as they cast their ballots this year, drawing on KFF analyses of findings from two national voter surveys. How health care issues factored into voters’ choices How abortion factored into voters’ choices Midterm Voters Give Democrats a Big Advantage to Handle Health Care What the Recent Elections and an Evolving Federal Policy Landscape Could Mean for Medicaid Expansion Efforts in 2027 What Does Democratic Control of Congress Mean for Global Health? Here’s What You Need To Know Frequently Asked Questions about the ACA’s Health Insurance Marketplace ACA Policies to See Another 13% Rise On Average for Premium Costs Next Year, and Other Things to Watch for the 2027 ACA Open Enrollment Period The ACA Marketplace Open Enrollment season began November 1, bringing higher out-of-pocket premium payments, new eligibility requirements for certain groups, and state efforts to offset premium increases following the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits. What could these and other changes mean for enrollees? Including the employers’ share, total annual premiums for family coverage now average $28,303, up 5% from 2025. Read the news release From Drew Altman: Are Employer Health Costs Out of Control? Abortion Recedes as a Motivator for Democratic Voters Even As Abortion Rights Prevail in Most Ballot Initiatives Nov 13, 2026 Quick Insights An analysis of midterm voter survey data shows that abortion played a smaller role in voters’ decisions to turn out compared to past elections, but abortion rights continues to draw broad support in most states when put directly to voters in ballot initiatives. The Advancing Global Health Annual Program Statement (AGH/APS) Mechanism: Supplementing the America First MOUs Nov 13, 2026 Issue Brief To shed greater light on U.S. global health efforts under the AFGHS, this analysis examines the Advancing Global Health APS (AGH/APS) award opportunities announced to date by looking at how funding may be directed across countries and selected areas of global health programming, painting a fuller picture of how continued U.S. global health investment may look in a post-USAID foreign aid landscape. Measles Elimination Status: What It Is and How the U.S. Could Lose It Nov 13, 2026 Policy Watch This policy watch examines the United States’ measles elimination status, including what it means to eliminate measles, whether the current measles outbreak could threaten the country’s measles elimination status, and what losing that status might mean for measles control. A Step Back for U.S. Public Health: The U.S. Is Likely to Lose Its Measles Elimination Status Nov 13, 2026 Quick Insights The loss of measles elimination status would primarily carry symbolic weight, as the effect of rising cases and deaths is already clear. Still, it is a marker of how a combination of factors - COVID-19, increasing vaccine skepticism, and a growing partisan divide about vaccines - has been a step back for public health, and it is not clear when or if this trend will be reversed. What the Recent Elections and an Evolving Federal Policy Landscape Could Mean for Medicaid Expansion Efforts in 2027 Nov 13, 2026 Policy Watch Among the ten states that have not adopted the Medicaid expansion, Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin are key states to watch for potential new debates about expansion given the outcome of the elections. Tracking Implementation of the 2025 Reconciliation Law: Medicaid Work Requirements Implementation Questions Nov 13, 2026 Other Post A list of the implementation questions relating to the Medicaid work requirements in the 2025 Reconciliation law. Tracking Implementation of the 2025 Reconciliation Law: Medicaid Work Requirements Nov 13, 2026 Feature KFF's interactive tracks key data and policies that will affect how states implement Medicaid work requirements, which are required under the 2025 budget reconciliation law starting in January 2027. The tracker includes state-level data on Medicaid enrollment and renewal outcomes as well as current state enrollment and renewal policies. initiatives. A Step Back for U.S. Public Health: The U.S. Is Likely to Lose Its Measles Elimination Status Nov 13, 2026 Quick Insights The loss of measles elimination status would primarily carry symbolic weight, as the effect of rising cases and deaths is already clear. news.content_title: Horizons from PBS News | U.S. struggles with measles surge after decades of progress
news.content: I'm William Brangham and this is "Horizons." Measles, it's an illness most of us have no memory of, even though infection was once a reality for almost every American child. Today, this highly contagious virus is making a resurgence with thousands of people infected this year. The return of measles coming up next. ♪ Narrator: Support for "Horizons" has been provided by Steve and Marilyn Kerman and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Additional support is provided by Friends of the News Hour. ♪ This program was made possible by contributions to your PBS station from viewers like you. Thank you. From the David M. Rubenstein Studio at WETA in Washington, here is William Brangham. Welcome to "Horizons." When it comes to measles, the U.S. is going backwards. Our country, once a global leader in our ability to contain this virus, is now seeing measles surge back. Officially, there have been almost 7,500 cases since January of last year, but many believe that number is a vast undercount. Eight people have died. Some tight-knit religious communities in Pennsylvania were the epicenter of this current wave, but there have been outbreaks in 46 states this year. New York declared a state of emergency over its outbreak. Measles, of course, is prevented with a vaccine, the MMR vaccine, specifically, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella. Over years of study, the MMR shot has proven to be a safe, effective, and lifesaving intervention. And while a majority of Americans still believe in the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a small but growing number of them are turning away from those tools. Childhood vaccination rates in the U.S. are in decline. The number of families choosing non-medical vaccine exemptions at school is rising. So to understand how we got here and where we go now, we turn to two experts in public health. Dr. William Schaffner is a professor of preventive medicine at Vanderbilt University and also teaches at its medical school in the Department of Infectious Diseases. Jessica Malaty Rivera is a public health epidemiologist. She writes the wonderful Substack column, "'Making Science Makes Sense." Thank you both so much to you two for being here. I'm going to ask you both this question, starting with you, Dr. Schaffner, first. In 2000, we eliminated this virus from the country through a public health and vaccination campaign. And yet now we have thousands of cases across the country. Eight people have died. Help us understand, how did we get to this moment? Well, William, I think it took some time for us to get here. And it's been a combination of reasons. First, perhaps a growing lack of trust in people of authority, including those of us in the medical profession. Other things that contributed were confusing recommendations coming from professional societies, but also from at least previously respected federal institutions, such as the CDC. We also have today people who wish to do things in a more natural way. It's also true that we now have a couple of generations, the parents and the grandparents who've never seen measles. And if you don't respect measles, you won't value the vaccines. And so they ask questions, why? And then lastly, I would say, and this may be a consequence of what happened during COVID, there are some people who just push back against obligations, mandates. In most states, in fact, in all states, in order to attend daycare and school, unless you have a medical and in some places, religious or personal belief exemption, you have to be vaccinated against measles. And some people just push back against that compulsion. Jessica Malaty Rivera, what would you add to that? Like we have, again, we've just gone through this tidal shift from having this virus at bay to now having it all over the place. What would you add to that about how we've gotten into this mess? You know, one of the things that concerns me is this normalization of pediatric disease. There seems to be a trend that is okay with disease, disability, and even death of children when it comes to childhood diseases like measles. So much so that there have been people who say that measles infection is good for you, that it could prevent cancer, which it cannot, that it's mild or just a rash, and it is neither mild or just a rash. And so I do worry that we have become accustomed to preventable suffering among a young and vulnerable population because of a commitment to individual freedom. We've kind of lost our way when it comes to the reasons why we vaccinate for viruses like measles, where we don't just do it to protect ourselves, we do it to protect those who cannot be vaccinated, which includes infants. Four of the eight deaths that have been reported this year have been among infants who were too young to be vaccinated. Those infants rely on their communities to be vaccinated so that measles doesn't spread. And I think that we've lost our way with that. I'd like to play a little bit of an interview that my colleague and I did with a doctor from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, she works in an emergency room there, about what they have been seeing in their community. This is Dr. Elizabeth Werley. Let's listen to what she told us. I'm Elizabeth Werley and I am the medical director of the emergency department at Penn State Health Lancaster Medical Center. And we are in the heart of the measles outbreak here in Lancaster County in Pennsylvania. For many of us in practice, we're only familiar with it from a textbook. So to actually witness and see what our patients are experiencing, they're in respiratory distress, they're having trouble breathing, they have significant GI symptoms. I do believe that lack of immunization is a factor in the current measles outbreak. We do have a large plain community here in Lancaster County and in Central Pennsylvania, but we also know it's out in the community, the general community as well. And even when other patients are immunized, we still have to worry about those patients that are at high risk, whether it is neonates who can't be immunized or those patients with other conditions or medications that put their immune system at risk. We have decades of information, both in our country and from other countries, demonstrating that the vaccinations are safe and they are effective. What I would tell someone if they're concerned about a measles exposure is to either get immunized if they have not been immunized, or they can have blood work with their primary care doctor to check their titers to see if their immunization still is active. And if they are experiencing symptoms that they are concerned about, that they should isolate at home and not go out into the community because of the high infectivity rate of the illness. It's very easy to spread. It can stay in the environment for a few hours afterwards. We have to take care of our community in addition to the patients that we're taking care of here in the hospital. I mean, it does put additional strains on an overworked healthcare system, and especially in emergency medicine, it's just one more thing that we have to be aware of to keep us on our toes. Dr. Schaffner, listening to her talk, there's so many factors in there. One of them that she was stressing is the contagiousness, the infectivity of this virus. For people who don't appreciate just how powerful this virus is, can you just remind us, how does it compare, say, to how easy it is to catch COVID or a cold? William, it is the most contagious virus that we know. One of the things she alluded to was a person who's shedding, breathes out the measles virus, can leave the room, and if a susceptible person comes into that room up to two hours later, they can still inhale the few viral particles that are hovering in the air and become infected and become ill. This is a virus that is extremely contagious, and obviously, that's why we want to vaccinate everyone. As Ms. Rivera said, we're protecting not only ourselves, our own children, our own families, but we're contributing to protection of everyone in the neighborhood and in our communities, because there are little babies who could get measles, and they have high mortality associated with that, who can't be vaccinated yet, and there are people who are immune-compromised. They can't take the vaccine. How do we protect them? All the rest of us are protected. We create a cocoon of protection around them so that the virus can't get to those most susceptible who live amongst us, our more frail brothers and sisters. Jessica, I mentioned that the official count, quote-unquote, "is 7,500 cases nationally this year." Do you think that that's an accurate picture of how widespread measles is in the country right now? I do not. I think that is a massive undercount, and I say that with confidence because if we've already seen eight deaths reported this year, which is a tragic milestone that we just hit this week, typically what you would see in a measles outbreak is one to three deaths per 1, 000 confirmed cases, so if you do a little bit of rough math, that would mean we would be well over 8000 cases to see a death rate at eight so far, and there's a few reasons for that. There is a slow-to-report sentiment in a lot of these closed communities. It is also just so massive that contact tracing and reporting is very overwhelming for departments of health. You have to recognize the fact that a measles outbreak is extremely resource-expensive for departments of health, both in the time and the personnel and even the cost of managing that size of an outbreak, and so I think it is much, much bigger than what we see right now. Dr. Schaffner, I'm curious, if someone is hearing all of this, worried about perhaps this very big undercount of measles, if they get vaccinated, how much protection does that offer you? Is this a bulletproof, 100% protection? How much does it give you? It's close to bulletproof. It's among the best vaccines we have. If you take the two recommended doses, you will get somewhere between 97% and 98% for likelihood of protection for the rest of your life, and even if you do happen to get a breakthrough infection, namely you're vaccinated, you're exposed, and you still get an infection, your illness will be milder, so this is a terrific vaccine in terms of effectiveness and it's also terrifically safe. There are very few adverse events associated with this vaccine. It's been used in the literal billions of doses around the world for 50 years now. Jessica Malaty Rivera, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. plays a complicated role here. At times, when asked about measles outbreaks, he has said, "Yes, go get vaccinated, "it will protect you," but in his previous career and in his current role in the federal government, he has done an enormous amount to sow distrust about vaccines and say that they are dangerous, they are harming people, that the government is not being square with people about this. How much responsibility do you place at the leadership of the federal government right now? I think he and the federal government bear a huge amount of responsibility because I think that this movement or this unprecedented outbreak didn't necessarily start at the beginning of it. There were seeds that were planted years and years ago by RFK Jr. himself and by people from his organization, his former organization, Children's Health Defense, and many like both of those actors who were sowing seeds of doubt about the MMR vaccine safety, the MMR vaccine's effectiveness, even the MMR vaccine's utility. And I think he would even say today that the only way to prevent the virus, the infection, is through the MMR vaccine. But what he's also saying is that it's okay to get it and it's okay to suffer for it because it's just a mild disease. And this is where I think that the normalization of disease has become so ubiquitous among people who are anti-MMR vaccine because they've been sold a lie. They've been sold a lie that it is something that can be treated with vitamin A and it cannot, that it's something that is typical for childhood when, you know, I'm grateful that I live in a time where my children don't have to experience a disease that was so prevalent back in the 80s. Even varicella is an example of that, that we have the tools to prevent them. Suffering can be avoided. It should not be the expectation simply because there are ways in which you could care for somebody. Now, it's also important to note there is no known, like, specific treatment for measles. It's all supportive care. And some kids will get pneumonia, and pneumonia is the number one cause of measles-related death. Some kids may get encephalitis. That is a very dangerous swelling of the brain that can cause a lot of permanent damage, including hearing loss and blindness and other impairments. It can cause complications years after recovery. And a rare encephalitis called SSPE can cause immune amnesia. These are not benign complications of a disease that is almost nearly entirely preventable through two doses of that vaccine. And RFK Jr. absolutely knows this, and it is the responsibility of the administration and our HHS secretary to make it extremely clear that kids do not have to be getting a very preventable disease. Dr. Schaffner, RFK Jr. has also suggested that vaccines, including MMR, cause a great deal of injury to individuals and that the government has not really done a good job of studying this. He's actually, under his leadership, set up a panel at the NIH to study vaccine injury in people. Is there any evidence of that? I mean, you mentioned before the safety record of this vaccine, but is there any evidence that the government knows that this is doing more damage to people and not telling us, or that these vaccines are complicated in any way? Well, William, before a vaccine is licensed, it is studied very, very carefully in large populations, not only how well it works, but whether it's safe. And then, more importantly, on an ongoing basis, after the vaccine is used, its safety continues to be monitored very carefully, not just by us, but by health departments, ministries of health around the world. And there is a uniformity of agreement that these vaccines are exceedingly safe. Adverse events associated with them, no vaccine, no pharmaceutical is perfect. They do occur rarely. And we have a compensation program that has been established in the United States to recognize those rare adverse events and provide at least some financial compensation to the families involved. So this has been thought about and studied with enormous care. If you look at the standard vaccine textbooks under measles vaccine, they have a whole large section under safety describing all of these studies that have been done. Brangham: Jessica Malaty Rivera, again, I can't help but know that we've got this ocean of misinformation out there. I just saw a study in JAMA this week that a survey of over 30,000 people and one in four Americans think that vaccines or taking Tylenol when you're pregnant is a major risk factor for autism. How do we...? As you write, making science makes sense. You are a science communicator. You're trying to help people understand the efficacy and safety of these. How do we go about combating this? It is so challenging. I can't deny the fact that this is incredibly difficult work, especially because even if the data are on our side, even if it was debunked, even if the paper that originally made the claim that connecting vaccines and specifically the MMR vaccine to autism was retracted, even if that person who wrote the paper had their medical license retracted as well or rescinded, it doesn't change the fact that something like that is incredibly sticky. And there's a lot of literature about the psychology and the dynamics of misinformation and why they stick, why they continue to spread and grow legs and continue to kind of morph into people's worldviews about public health. This is one of those things that has unfortunately remained very, very strong in people's minds when it comes to vaccine safety. And I think it is partially because it evokes a lot of fear. A lot of the misinformation that we see based on vaccines is intended to cause a very intense emotional reaction. And it dysregulates people. And dysregulated people consuming more misinformation just causes an information ecosystem that becomes even more difficult for trained and untrained eyes to decipher what is true and what is not true. We're dealing with people who are outside of their expertise opining on issues about vaccinology, about immunology, about infectious diseases, but said with conviction, said with identifying features that seem connected to the audience, whether that be a person who's a parent, whether that be a person who's an advocate, those types of things kind of suspend the facts, unfortunately. So even if the data on our side, and I'll kind of reiterate too, that there are... I can't think of a vaccine that is more scrutinized than the MMR vaccine, other than the COVID-19 vaccine, in which we've specifically looked into it to see if it has any credibility, this claim about MMR and autism. They've done massive studies comparing siblings, comparing twins, comparing people from across populations in different vaccine schedules, simply to say, "Can we confidently prove "that there is an association or even a link?" And we have not been able to do that. And so unfortunately, emotions and anecdotes outweigh data in situations like this, which is why storytelling and empathy in your science communication have to be part of your strategy, because at this point, you're not dealing with facts against facts. I'm going to do a couple of all of that. Just to expand on that, if I may just quickly, we tend to give our patients facts that goes to your brain, but the behavioral psychologists have told us, just as Jessica has mentioned, that how we…
