You know, one of the things that concerns me is this normalization of pediatric disease. There seems to be a trend that is okay with disease, disability, and even death of children when it comes to childhood diseases like measles. So much so that there have been people who say that measles infection is good for you, that it could prevent cancer, which it cannot, that it's mild or just a rash, and it is neither mild or just a rash. And so I do worry that we have become accustomed to preventable suffering among a young and vulnerable population because of a commitment to individual freedom. We've kind of lost our way when it comes to the reasons why we vaccinate for viruses like measles, where we don't just do it to protect ourselves, we do it to protect those who cannot be vaccinated, which includes infants. Four of the eight deaths that have been reported this year have been among infants who were too young to be vaccinated. Those infants rely on their communities to be vaccinated so that measles doesn't spread. And I think that we've lost our way with that. I'd like to play a little bit of an interview that my colleague and I did with a doctor from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, she works in an emergency room there, about what they have been seeing in their community. This is Dr. Elizabeth Werley. Let's listen to what she told us. I'm Elizabeth Werley and I am the medical director of the emergency department at Penn State Health Lancaster Medical Center. And we are in the heart of the measles outbreak here in Lancaster County in Pennsylvania. For many of us in practice, we're only familiar with it from a textbook. So to actually witness and see what our patients are experiencing, they're in respiratory distress, they're having trouble breathing, they have significant GI symptoms. I do believe that lack of immunization is a factor in the current measles outbreak. We do have a large plain community here in Lancaster County and in Central Pennsylvania, but we also know it's out in the community, the general community as well. And even when other patients are immunized, we still have to worry about those patients that are at high risk, whether it is neonates who can't be immunized or those patients with other conditions or medications that put their immune system at risk. We have decades of information, both in our country and from other countries, demonstrating that the vaccinations are safe and they are effective. What I would tell someone if they're concerned about a measles exposure is to either get immunized if they have not been immunized, or they can have blood work with their primary care doctor to check their titers to see if their immunization still is active. And if they are experiencing symptoms that they are concerned about, that they should isolate at home and not go out into the community because of the high infectivity rate of the illness. It's very easy to spread. It can stay in the environment for a few hours afterwards. We have to take care of our community in addition to the patients that we're taking care of here in the hospital. I mean, it does put additional strains on an overworked healthcare system, and especially in emergency medicine, it's just one more thing that we have to be aware of to keep us on our toes. Dr. Schaffner, listening to her talk, there's so many factors in there. One of them that she was stressing is the contagiousness, the infectivity of this virus. For people who don't appreciate just how powerful this virus is, can you just remind us, how does it compare, say, to how easy it is to catch COVID or a cold? William, it is the most contagious virus that we know. One of the things she alluded to was a person who's shedding, breathes out the measles virus, can leave the room, and if a susceptible person comes into that room up to two hours later, they can still inhale the few viral particles that are hovering in the air and become infected and become ill. This is a virus that is extremely contagious, and obviously, that's why we want to vaccinate everyone. As Ms. Rivera said, we're protecting not only ourselves, our own children, our own families, but we're contributing to protection of everyone in the neighborhood and in our communities, because there are little babies who could get measles, and they have high mortality associated with that, who can't be vaccinated yet, and there are people who are immune-compromised. They can't take the vaccine. How do we protect them? All the rest of us are protected. We create a cocoon of protection around them so that the virus can't get to those most susceptible who live amongst us, our more frail brothers and sisters. Jessica, I mentioned that the official count, quote-unquote, "is 7,500 cases nationally this year." Do you think that that's an accurate picture of how widespread measles is in the country right now? I do not. I think that is a massive undercount, and I say that with confidence because if we've already seen eight deaths reported this year, which is a tragic milestone that we just hit this week, typically what you would see in a measles outbreak is one to three deaths per 1, 000 confirmed cases, so if you do a little bit of rough math, that would mean we would be well over 8000 cases to see a death rate at eight so far, and there's a few reasons for that. There is a slow-to-report sentiment in a lot of these closed communities. It is also just so massive that contact tracing and reporting is very overwhelming for departments of health. You have to recognize the fact that a measles outbreak is extremely resource-expensive for departments of health, both in the time and the personnel and even the cost of managing that size of an outbreak, and so I think it is much, much bigger than what we see right now. Dr. Schaffner, I'm curious, if someone is hearing all of this, worried about perhaps this very big undercount of measles, if they get vaccinated, how much protection does that offer you? Is this a bulletproof, 100% protection? How much does it give you? It's close to bulletproof. It's among the best vaccines we have. If you take the two recommended doses, you will get somewhere between 97% and 98% for likelihood of protection for the rest of your life, and even if you do happen to get a breakthrough infection, namely you're vaccinated, you're exposed, and you still get an infection, your illness will be milder, so this is a terrific vaccine in terms of effectiveness and it's also terrifically safe. There are very few adverse events associated with this vaccine. It's been used in the literal billions of doses around the world for 50 years now. Jessica Malaty Rivera, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. plays a complicated role here. At times, when asked about measles outbreaks, he has said, "Yes, go get vaccinated, "it will protect you," but in his previous career and in his current role in the federal government, he has done an enormous amount to sow distrust about vaccines and say that they are dangerous, they are harming people, that the government is not being square with people about this. How much responsibility do you place at the leadership of the federal government right now? I think he and the federal government bear a huge amount of responsibility because I think that this movement or this unprecedented outbreak didn't necessarily start at the beginning of it. There were seeds that were planted years and years ago by RFK Jr. himself and by people from his organization, his former organization, Children's Health Defense, and many like both of those actors who were sowing seeds of doubt about the MMR vaccine safety, the MMR vaccine's effectiveness, even the MMR vaccine's utility. And I think he would even say today that the only way to prevent the virus, the infection, is through the MMR vaccine. But what he's also saying is that it's okay to get it and it's okay to suffer for it because it's just a mild disease. And this is where I think that the normalization of disease has become so ubiquitous among people who are anti-MMR vaccine because they've been sold a lie. They've been sold a lie that it is something that can be treated with vitamin A and it cannot, that it's something that is typical for childhood when, you know, I'm grateful that I live in a time where my children don't have to experience a disease that was so prevalent back in the 80s. Even varicella is an example of that, that we have the tools to prevent them. Suffering can be avoided. It should not be the expectation simply because there are ways in which you could care for somebody. Now, it's also important to note there is no known, like, specific treatment for measles. It's all supportive care. And some kids will get pneumonia, and pneumonia is the number one cause of measles-related death. Some kids may get encephalitis. That is a very dangerous swelling of the brain that can cause a lot of permanent damage, including hearing loss and blindness and other impairments. It can cause complications years after recovery. And a rare encephalitis called SSPE can cause immune amnesia. These are not benign complications of a disease that is almost nearly entirely preventable through two doses of that vaccine. And RFK Jr. absolutely knows this, and it is the responsibility of the administration and our HHS secretary to make it extremely clear that kids do not have to be getting a very preventable disease. Dr. Schaffner, RFK Jr. has also suggested that vaccines, including MMR, cause a great deal of injury to individuals and that the government has not really done a good job of studying this. He's actually, under his leadership, set up a panel at the NIH to study vaccine injury in people. Is there any evidence of that? I mean, you mentioned before the safety record of this vaccine, but is there any evidence that the government knows that this is doing more damage to people and not telling us, or that these vaccines are complicated in any way? Well, William, before a vaccine is licensed, it is studied very, very carefully in large populations, not only how well it works, but whether it's safe. And then, more importantly, on an ongoing basis, after the vaccine is used, its safety continues to be monitored very carefully, not just by us, but by health departments, ministries of health around the world. And there is a uniformity of agreement that these vaccines are exceedingly safe. Adverse events associated with them, no vaccine, no pharmaceutical is perfect. They do occur rarely. And we have a compensation program that has been established in the United States to recognize those rare adverse events and provide at least some financial compensation to the families involved. So this has been thought about and studied with enormous care. If you look at the standard vaccine textbooks under measles vaccine, they have a whole large section under safety describing all of these studies that have been done. Brangham: Jessica Malaty Rivera, again, I can't help but know that we've got this ocean of misinformation out there. I just saw a study in JAMA this week that a survey of over 30,000 people and one in four Americans think that vaccines or taking Tylenol when you're pregnant is a major risk factor for autism. How do we...? As you write, making science makes sense. You are a science communicator. You're trying to help people understand the efficacy and safety of these. How do we go about combating this? It is so challenging. I can't deny the fact that this is incredibly difficult work, especially because even if the data are on our side, even if it was debunked, even if the paper that originally made the claim that connecting vaccines and specifically the MMR vaccine to autism was retracted, even if that person who wrote the paper had their medical license retracted as well or rescinded, it doesn't change the fact that something like that is incredibly sticky. And there's a lot of literature about the psychology and the dynamics of misinformation and why they stick, why they continue to spread and grow legs and continue to kind of morph into people's worldviews about public health. This is one of those things that has unfortunately remained very, very strong in people's minds when it comes to vaccine safety. And I think it is partially because it evokes a lot of fear. A lot of the misinformation that we see based on vaccines is intended to cause a very intense emotional reaction. And it dysregulates people. And dysregulated people consuming more misinformation just causes an information ecosystem that becomes even more difficult for trained and untrained eyes to decipher what is true and what is not true. We're dealing with people who are outside of their expertise opining on issues about vaccinology, about immunology, about infectious diseases, but said with conviction, said with identifying features that seem connected to the audience, whether that be a person who's a parent, whether that be a person who's an advocate, those types of things kind of suspend the facts, unfortunately. So even if the data on our side, and I'll kind of reiterate too, that there are... I can't think of a vaccine that is more scrutinized than the MMR vaccine, other than the COVID-19 vaccine, in which we've specifically looked into it to see if it has any credibility, this claim about MMR and autism. They've done massive studies comparing siblings, comparing twins, comparing people from across populations in different vaccine schedules, simply to say, "Can we confidently prove "that there is an association or even a link?" And we have not been able to do that. And so unfortunately, emotions and anecdotes outweigh data in situations like this, which is why storytelling and empathy in your science communication have to be part of your strategy, because at this point, you're not dealing with facts against facts. I'm going to do a couple of all of that. Just to expand on that, if I may just quickly, we tend to give our patients facts that goes to your brain, but the behavioral psychologists have told us, just as Jessica has mentioned, that how we...

news.title_zh: 麻疹:它是什么、它如何传播以及如果您怀疑它该怎么办 - EMS1
news.source_body_en: This article from EMS1, published on November 09, 2026, discusses the resurgence of measles in the United States, highlighting outbreaks in recent years, particularly in under-immunized communities. It notes that measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000 but has seen notable surges, such as the 2014 Disneyland outbreak and the 2019 outbreaks in the Pacific Northwest and New York City. The article outlines the stages of measles infection, its symptoms, and prevention strategies, including the MMR vaccine, which is 99% effective when both doses are given. It also provides a 5-step guide for emergency responders handling potential measles cases, emphasizing the importance of PPE, symptoms assessment, and isolation protocols. The CDC recommends the first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12–15 months and the second at 4–6 years. Parents are advised to watch for severe symptoms such as high fever, difficulty breathing, or neurological issues and seek immediate medical care if necessary. The article does not report specific case counts or deaths for the current outbreak but highlights the historical impact of measles, with an estimated 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations annually before the vaccine's introduction in 1963. The information is based on the CDC and Johns Hopkins University, and the article serves as a guide for public awareness and emergency response.

Facilities & Rentals WOSU Events Calendar Facilities & Rentals Airfare Health, Science & Environment Measles cases pass 300 in Ohio as US is poised to lose elimination status Ideastream Public Media | By Ida Lieszkovszky Published November 10, 2026 at 11:12 AM EST Facebook Threads Twitter LinkedIn Email Leigh Prather / Adobe Stock Images According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. There have been 310 confirmed cases of measles in Ohio since January, as the measles epidemic continues to spread nationwide. Ashtabula, Geauga and Wayne counties account for roughly half of all cases statewide. As of Nov. 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 5,182 cases across the country. The spike in measles comes as the Pan American Health Organization convenes a meeting to determine the measles and rubella elimination status of the Americas. The U.S. is at risk of losing its measles elimination status. Losing elimination status happens when a country cannot stop the spread of measles over a 12-month period. Put another way, measles is considered endemic in a country if there is continuous transmission over a 12-month period. The U.S. has been dealing with a series of measles outbreaks since early 2025. Canada lost its measles elimination status last year. The best thing people can do to protect themselves from measles is to make sure they’re fully vaccinated, according to Dr. Claudia Hoyen, the director of pediatric infection control at University Hospitals’ Rainbow Babies Children’s. “Measles is not just a rash. There can be pretty significant complications,” she said. “One in 20 kids will end up with pneumonia and potentially in the hospital. We worry terribly about complications like encephalitis, which you can get if you have the measles.” Encephalitis is an inflammation of the brain tissue. Measles can also lead to dangerous long-term complications, including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), which is a rare but fatal degenerative disease. SSPE can take between seven and 15 years to emerge after an initial measles infection and is particularly dangerous when children catch measles at a young age, especially under 2. It is not caused by the MMR vaccine. Ohio Department of Health Geauga county has recorded 54 cases of measles in 2026, and Ashtabula another 47. The MMR vaccine is typically given in two doses during childhood. Hoyen said older adults can check with their doctors if they’re concerned about their immunity level. “I think the best thing that people can do is understand what their immunity is,” she said. "Once you have that immunity then that's a good thing because it's going to keep you protected.” Two doses of the MMR vaccine leads to 97% protection against measles. According to the CDC, 96% of the measles cases nationwide are in people who are either unvaccinated or whose vaccine status is unknown. Hoyen said there are interventions that can help minimize the complications associated with measles in unvaccinated individuals. Getting the MMR vaccine within the first three days of contracting measles can help prevent infection or reduce the severity of the illness. She said for people who are immunocompromised or pregnant, there are immunoglobulin treatments available to help protect against complications. Experts are asking people who think they may have been exposed to the measles virus or are experiencing symptoms associated with measles to call ahead to their local hospital rather than just walking into a doctor’s office or the emergency room. That’s because the measles virus can linger in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected individual has left a space. It can take seven to 14 days for symptoms to emerge after an initial exposure. Measles symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes. It’s also typically accompanied by white spots that can appear inside the mouth and a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward on the body. There have been several local warnings of potential measles exposures in Northeast Ohio. Akron Children’s Hospital warned the public of a possible measles exposure at the Golisano Campus on Oct. 20. Health officials also warned of a possible exposure at SweetBerry Fresh Market in Wickliffe on Oct. 3, 5, or 6. In Warren, officials warned of a possible exposure at Mercy Health St. Joseph Warren Hospital’s emergency room on Aug. 23. By Ida Lieszkovszky Published November 10, 2026 at 11:12 AM EST Facebook Threads Twitter LinkedIn Email Leigh Prather / Adobe Stock Images According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. There have been 310 confirmed cases of measles in Ohio since January, as the measles epidemic continues to spread nationwide. Ashtabula, Geauga and Wayne counties account for roughly half of all cases statewide. As of Nov. 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 5,182 cases across the country. The spike in measles comes as the Pan American Health Organization convenes a meeting to determine the measles and rubella elimination status of the Americas. The U.S. is at risk of losing its measles elimination status. Losing elimination status happens when a country cannot stop the spread of measles over a 12-month period. Put another way, measles is considered endemic in a country if there is continuous transmission over a 12-month period. The U.S. has been dealing with a series of measles outbreaks since early 2025. Canada lost its measles elimination status last year. The best thing people can do to protect themselves from measles is to make sure they’re fully vaccinated, according to Dr. Claudia Hoyen, the director of pediatric infection control at University Hospitals’ Rainbow Babies Children’s. “Measles is not just a rash. There can be pretty significant complications,” she said. “One in 20 kids will end up with pneumonia and potentially in the hospital. We worry terribly about complications like encephalitis, which you can get if you have the measles.” Encephalitis is an inflammation of the brain tissue. Measles can also lead to dangerous long-term complications, including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), which is a rare but fatal degenerative disease. SSPE can take between seven and 15 years to emerge after an initial measles infection and is particularly dangerous when children catch measles at a young age, especially under 2. It is not caused by the MMR vaccine. Ohio Department of Health Geauga county has recorded 54 cases of measles in 2026, and Ashtabula another 47. The MMR vaccine is typically given in two doses during childhood. Hoyen said older adults can check with their doctors if they’re concerned about their immunity level. “I think the best thing that people can do is understand what their immunity is,” she said. "Once you have that immunity then that's a good thing because it's going to keep you protected.” Two doses of the MMR vaccine leads to 97% protection against measles. According to the CDC, 96% of the measles cases nationwide are in people who are either unvaccinated or whose vaccine status is unknown. Hoyen said there are interventions that can help minimize the complications associated with measles in unvaccinated individuals. Getting the MMR vaccine within the first three days of contracting measles can help prevent infection or reduce the severity of the illness. She said for people who are immunocompromised or pregnant, there are immunoglobulin treatments available to help protect against complications. Experts are asking people who think they may have been exposed to the measles virus or are experiencing symptoms associated with measles to call ahead to their local hospital rather than just walking into a doctor’s office or the emergency room. That’s because the measles virus can linger in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected individual has left a space. It can take seven to 14 days for symptoms to emerge after an initial exposure. Measles symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes. It’s also typically accompanied by white spots that can appear inside the mouth and a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward on the body. There have been several local warnings of potential measles exposures in Northeast Ohio. Akron Children’s Hospital warned the public of a possible measles exposure at the Golisano Campus on Oct. 20. Health officials also warned of a possible exposure at SweetBerry Fresh Market in Wickliffe on Oct. 3, 5, or 6. In Warren, officials warned of a possible exposure at Mercy Health St. Joseph Warren Hospital’s emergency room on Aug. 23. (WBAY) - The Wisconsin Department of Health Services and the Grant County Health Department confirmed a pediatric measles-associated death in Wisconsin, the second death connected to the state’s measles outbreak in 2026. To protect the privacy of the family and the child, DHS said it will not release any additional information about the death. Case counts As of Nov. 13, 2026, DHS has reported 649 measles cases in 20 counties since August 2026. DHS said this is the highest number of cases in the state in more than 35 years. Reported case counts may not reflect the full extent of measles spread. Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means some cases may go unreported. Anyone can become seriously ill. Children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications. State response DHS continues to work with local and Tribal health departments and health care partners to coordinate and support the statewide response. The efforts include supporting case identification and tracking, information sharing, testing and vaccination. Since Aug. 1, 2026, DHS has delivered nearly 2,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine to local health departments in communities with confirmed cases, and it is making additional doses available. Over 45,600 total doses of MMR vaccine have been administered by local public health agencies and health care providers in Wisconsin during this time. “Preventing the spread of measles takes action from all of us,” said State Health Officer and Division of Public Health Administrator Paula Tran. “From making sure our families are protected by getting the recommended vaccinations to staying home when we may have been exposed, we encourage everyone to work together to protect those who are most vulnerable to serious illness. Stay informed, look out for one another, and take the actions you can to help stop the spread of measles and keep our communities healthy and safe.” Vaccination The best way to prevent measles is with the MMR vaccine. Two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles. Wisconsin residents can check their vaccination records online using the Wisconsin Immunization Registry. They can also contact their health care provider or local health department. If you are exposed DHS advises anyone who has been exposed to measles to stay home. People who develop a fever and rash, especially if they have been exposed to measles or are not vaccinated, should contact their health care provider, DHS said. news.content: FAA says it has lifted nationwide ground stop that snarled airports Friday News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE One person may have spread measles at a half-dozen sites in Ohio Chad Murphy USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Nov. 12, 2026, 12:07 p.m. ET A confirmed measles case may have led to multiple being exposed at several locations in Northeast Ohio. Health officials have released a list of potential exposure sites in Geauga and Lake counties, including two schools and two restaurants. Ohio has seen a nearly 600% increase in measles cases this year compared to all of last year. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among individuals who are not vaccinated. The measles vaccine is 97% effective, and vaccination is the best way to prevent the disease. One person infected with measles may have spread the highly contagious disease over a period of about a week at more than a half-dozen sites in Northeast Ohio. Geauga Public Health is reporting a confirmed case of measles with exposures at several public locations in Geauga and Lake counties during the time period the individual was able to spread the virus. Statewide, the Ohio Department of Health is reporting 310 cases in 25 counties so far this year, according to its most recent summary of infectious diseases dashboard update on Nov. 5. That number is nearly six times (588.9%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Here's where measles may have spread in Geauga and Lake counties. Here's where people may have been exposed to the measles virus in Lake and Geauga counties According to Geauga Public Health, people may have been exposed to measles during these dates and times, and at these locations: Monday Nov. 2 to Thursday Nov. 5, from about 7:45 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Berkshire Middle School, 14155 Claridon Troy Road, Burton, Ohio Tuesday Nov. 3, from about 3:30 to 7 p.m. Kent State University - Geauga Campus, 14111 Claridon Troy Road, Burton, Ohio Tuesday, Nov. 3 and Thursday Nov. 5, during evening (dinner) hours The Hambone, 13960 Rock Creek Road, Chardon, Ohio Tuesday Nov. 3, from about 5:30 to 9:30 p.m. Berkshire Local Schools Fall Choir Concert, 14155 Claridon Troy Road, Burton, Ohio Friday, Nov. 6, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. SPC Sports, 9431 Mentor Ave., Mentor, Ohio Friday, Nov. 6, from about 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Longhorn Steakhouse, 9557 Mentor Ave., Mentor, Ohio Saturday, Nov. 7, from 5:54 to 8:48 p.m. University Hospitals Urgent Care Concord, 7500 Auburn Road, Suite 1200, Concord, Ohio Can you get measles if you have been vaccinated? Two doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. past last year's totals By FOX 5 Atlanta Digital Team FOX 5 Atlanta Georgia Published November 10, 2026 8:54 PM EST Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published November 10, 2026 8:54 PM EST The Brief State health officials confirmed three new measles cases in Macon County linked to an earlier October exposure. The latest infections raise Georgia's total count to 28 cases, nearly tripling the state's tally recorded throughout 2025. Health leaders urge anyone displaying measles symptoms to contact medical providers by telephone before visiting clinics or emergency facilities. MACON, Ga. - Three new measles cases have been confirmed in Macon County among people exposed to a previous patient, state health officials announced Tuesday. Macon County measles outbreak What we know: The Georgia Department of Public Health confirmed the three individuals contracted the virus after coming into close contact with a person diagnosed on Oct. 12. Agency staff members have notified other community members who may have faced exposure and carry an elevated risk of falling ill. Dermatologists Beg Women With Thin Hair To Use This Household ItemTop Austin Hairstylist | SponsoredSponsored Learn More Undo The three diagnoses bring the total count across Georgia to 28 confirmed cases, according to state health records. That figure marks a sharp climb from 2025, which saw 10 cases reported statewide during the entire year. Preventing measles virus exposure What we don't know: Health authorities have not identified the specific public locations where possible community exposures occurred or the current condition of the three patients. Officials also have not released the ages or vaccination status of the individuals who tested positive. The Georgia Department of Public Health advises anyone experiencing symptoms to call a doctor's office, hospital, or public health clinic ahead of time rather than arriving unannounced. Calling in advance prevents the virus from spreading through healthcare waiting areas. Measles in Georgia Timeline: Georgia has experienced a sharp uptick in measles cases since late summer, jumping from seven confirmed infections in mid-August to 25 by late October, according to the Georgia Department of Public Health. That total more than doubles the 10 infections recorded across the state in all of 2025. The surge began on Aug. 18 when state health officials confirmed that an unvaccinated metro Atlanta resident tested positive with no reported travel history or known exposure. Within days, transmission spread into a childcare center, leading to four confirmed pediatric cases on Aug. 28 and three additional cases on Sept. 4 linked to the daycare cluster. Outbreaks widened beyond the metro area in the weeks that followed. On Sept. 30, state epidemiologists verified that five siblings in Jasper County contracted the virus following out-of-state travel. By mid-October, cases emerged in central Georgia when an unvaccinated Macon County resident tested positive following exposure to a visitor linked to a broader outbreak in Pennsylvania. The infection triggered a public health exposure alert for patrons of a Perry steakhouse on Oct. 19, followed on Oct. 27 by three additional positive tests among the resident's close contacts. State public health officials noted that nearly all of the confirmed patients were unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated against the airborne virus. Protecting families through vaccination Dig deeper: Medical professionals emphasize that immunization remains the most reliable defense against the disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends children receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, targeting measles, mumps and rubella. Under federal guidelines, pediatricians administer the first shot between 12 and 15 months of age, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. Parents seeking information about immunization schedules can consult their personal healthcare providers or visit public health portals provided by state and federal health agencies. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from a news release issued by the Georgia Department of Public Health and guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Doctor Urges Anyone Over 60 With Constipation to Drink 1 Cup of This News/Commentary Babies are getting measles in the womb. That wasn’t a problem before the vaccine, pediatricians say November 11, 2026 | Libby Bandelin | Print Article Share Tweet Truth Gettr Telegram A blue state recently reported an alarming rise of infants born with measles and pushed vaccination — these cases may be the result of lost natural immunization after the introduction of the MMR vaccine, doctors say. The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) issued an alert about an increase in measles cases during pregnancy on Oct. 19, and confirmed that 66 mothers had come down with the disease and at least six babies were born with it in Pennsylvania throughout 2026, doctors told NBC. While the DOH said that day in a press release that getting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine “is the best way to prevent measles and newborn measles,” some pediatricians and family practice doctors disagree, according to an article published Monday in the Defender, Children’s Health Defense‘s news source. Doctors who spoke with the outlet said that congenital measles — when a baby is born with the disease passed down by his or her mother in utero — used to be a rare occurrence before the vaccine was introduced more than 50 years ago. They added that decades of research shows that vaccine-induced immunity is weaker than natural immunity to the measles disease. SilverPenny “For the first time in a generation, American babies are being born infected with measles and the science told us this was coming,” Michelle Perro, a pediatrician told the Defender. “The vaccine program didn’t eliminate measles — it shifted the risk to the most vulnerable: newborns and the pregnant women carrying them.” These physicians claim that women who had a natural measles infection as a child are better protected against giving birth to a baby with congenital measles than women who got the MMR vaccine, the Defender reported. The MMR vaccine was first introduced to the United States’ markets in 1971 as a combined measles, mumps and rubella shot, however it did not get widely adopted until the 1980’s when the World Health Organization starting expanding vaccination initiatives, according to the WHO. Before the MMR vaccine, measles was a “routine childhood illness,” where over 99 percent of children made it through the disease with “no problem, resulting in robust, permanent and life-long immunity,” family practitioner Dr. Ben Edwards told the Defender. The Pennsylvania Department of Health was not able to provide comment to the DCNF before publication. “Practically all pregnant mothers had measles in their youth,” Edwards said to the outlet. “It’s really a beautifully designed natural immunization process — but we’ve lost that because of the measles vaccine program.” ADVERTISEMENT Around the Web Protein Isn't Enough - Here's What Really Builds Muscle After 60 ApexLabs Edwards runs a private practice serving roughly 2,000 patients and treated over 300 cases of measles during the West Texas measles outbreak, the defender reported. Edwards said that before the vaccine, mothers passed along protective antibodies to their babies in the womb, which protected the babies during the “more vulnerable first year of life.” Children would get measles sometime in the first decades of life and then develop their own robust, lifelong immunity, the doctor told the Defender. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) also acknowledges that congenital measles was exceedingly rare before the introduction of the MMR vaccine, the outlet reported. “Historical studies suggest that congenital measles was uncommon in the prevaccine era, when most pregnant women were previously infected with measles during childhood,” the AAP said in a FAQ about congenital measles. The AAP defines congenital measles as an infection acquired before birth in which a newborn tests positive for measles or develops symptoms within the first 10 days of life. There’s about a 25 percent to 30 percent chance a pregnant woman who contracts measles will transmit the virus to her unborn child, the AAP said. Yifare Pennsylvania continues to boast high numbers of measles cases, with 1,487 confirmed reports and six measles or “measles-associated” deaths as of Nov. 6, the Defender reported. Two of these deaths were reportedly of infants, but it is unknown whether they had congenital infections, according to the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy (CIDRAP). Pennsylvania’s death count included a stillborn baby who tested positive for measles, suggesting a case of congenital measles, as Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro announced during an August press conference. However, the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, told the Philadelphia Inquirer the child died of a ruptured spleen — not from measles. news.content_title: Pennsylvania sees growing number of measles cases among pregnant women
news.content: Close the sidebar Video Wellness Style Family Food Culture Living Shop Close the sidebar Menu ABC News Parenting November 10, 2026 Measles cases grow among pregnant women in Pennsylvania: What to know about risks WATCH: Measles cases top 5,000 as US set to lose elimination status By Dr. Jade Cobern Measles cases in Pennsylvania have now surpassed 1,500, according to data reported on Monday. As the outbreak continues to grow, doctors and health officials are concerned about a rising number of cases among pregnant women, posing a risk to both mom and baby. As of Nov. 6, "the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) has now confirmed that 97 of the state's measles cases in 2026 were in pregnant women," Stephanie Nojiri, the DOH deputy press secretary, told ABC News. There were only 16 total measles cases in the state in 2025 and 6 total in 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). "Because measles was declared eliminated in the United States decades ago, modern data related to measles during pregnancy and the related risks is limited, but clinical studies and systematic reviews provide clear statistical evidence of the dangers associated with contracting measles while pregnant," the PA DOH said in a statement. "The 97 cases of measles confirmed in pregnant women thus far in 2026 is the highest number of cases in that demographic in Pennsylvania in decades," the state department of health said. "Pennsylvania has not seen an overall outbreak of this size in 35 years." The department added it "has provided clinical consultation for pregnant women with measles throughout the outbreak." The PA DOH released guidance about measles in pregnancy in a health alert last month. In addition to posing a risk to the mother's health, measles infection in pregnancy can be transmitted to the baby before birth, leading to congenital measles. Risks of measles to mom and baby The CDC warns that measles infection during pregnancy can lead to complications including pneumonia and death, as well as pregnancy loss, premature delivery, and low birth weight for their babies. "You have to watch the mother fetus dyad so closely because of the risk of fetal death," Dr. Sharee Livingston, an OBGYN at UPMC Magee-Womens in Central Pennsylvania, told ABC News. "You're paying attention to things like growth restriction and ensuring that there's fetal well-being, so that you can intervene with delivery if the fetus is viable." Livingston said she has taken care of several pregnant women with measles in this outbreak. "That's a scary place to be for the patient, for the supporter, for the healthcare provider to know that you have a person with a communicable disease that is preventable, and that could put both her and her fetus at risk," Livingston said. "It's a very challenging position to be in." If transmitted in utero, a baby can be born with congenital measles, "characterized by a febrile rash syndrome within 10 days of birth," the CDC says. These babies are at risk of many health complications including pneumonia, encephalitis, and death. Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, said the risk of congenial measles is highest when the baby is delivered within 10 days of the mother developing a rash from measles. If the baby survives in the short term, a congenital measles infection places them at higher risk of later developing a progressive and fatal neurological condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), the CDC says. SSPE is characterized by "a deterioration in social skills, deterioration in personality, deterioration in handwriting. You descend into a vegetative state and die," Offit said. "The difference for congenital measles is you don't have to wait five or seven years. It can happen in a few months. It can happen within two years." Overall, cases of congenital measles have been very rare in the United States. Offit explained that congenital measles has historically been very rare because most adults were immune to the virus from infection in childhood before widespread immunization. "We're learning about congenital measles. We really are," Offit said. "In the measles era, meaning before the [1963] vaccine ... Children would get infected, so they wouldn't get infected as adults." Now, Offit said we are seeing the impacts of a growing adult population who are not immune to the virus. "You have people in their 20s, 30s, and 40s now who really didn't grow up in the age of measles," Offit said. "They are extremely unlikely they would have been naturally infected, and they've chosen not to vaccinate. So now, what you have that I didn't have when I was a child was a fairly large population of vulnerable adults." Tracking cases of congenital measles is also complicated by lack of standardized reporting in the U.S. The PA DOH said in a statement there is "no national public health case definition for standardized reporting or tracking of congenital measles cases." The department added, "DOH is working closely with our colleagues at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to develop standard definitions and tracking tools for congenital measles cases." Treatment and prevention The CDC says pregnant women should not receive the MMR vaccine because it contains some live virus, but they can receive immunoglobulin antibodies. This can reduce the risk of infection if they are non-immune and exposed to measles in pregnancy or to help lessen the severity of illness if infected. There is no specific treatment for congenital measles, but newborns can also receive immunoglobulin if they are born to a mother with measles which may help lessen the severity or risk of death from congenital measles, the CDC says. Dr. Holly W. Cummings, an OBGYN and chair of the Pennsylvania section of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said that preconception counseling about vaccines is very important to help prevent more pregnant women from getting measles. "Optimum pregnancy care for everybody, even outside of the context of a measles outbreak, is to have preconception care," Cummings said. "See your healthcare provider before you get pregnant, so that you can talk about any health planning that needs to be taken into account before pregnancy. One of those things we routinely think about before pregnancy is vaccination status." It is also recommended for the people around pregnant women and young babies to be up to date on vaccines too, adding an extra layer of protection for them. "If you're a family member with a pregnant woman in your family, she would no longer be able to be vaccinated, but other people in the family could be," Cummings said. "So that's the next best thing for creating a safe environment for the pregnant woman and the unborn fetus and the eventual baby that's going to join the family." Jade A. Cobern, MD, MPH, is a practicing physician, board-certified in pediatrics and general preventive medicine, and is a fellow of the ABC News Medical Unit. Dr. Elizabeth Herrin also contributed to this story. news.content: Nationwide ground stop caused by aging, 'overloaded' air traffic control systems, officials say Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTH Ohio Department of Health Add Topic Measles spreads again in Ohio as US may soon lose elimination status Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Nov. 13, 2026, 11:10 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with cases increasing by 21% in the past week. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, putting the country's measles elimination status at risk. Health officials state the MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent measles, which can be a deadly disease. As one person may have spread measles across seven locations in two Ohio counties, yet another county joined the list of confirmed cases as the state's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. And the United States is in danger of losing its measles elimination status as the World Health Organization was set to meet. Ohio added 17 new cases in the past week, a 21% increase from the 14 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 327 cases in 26 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Nov. 12. That number is more than six times (626.7%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Mahoning County joined the list this week with one case, and Ashtabula reported the most new cases with six. Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. As of Nov. 5, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 5,182 confirmed measles cases in 45 states plus Washington, D.C. – more than double last year's total of 2,289, USA TODAY reports. That's the highest annual total since 1991. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 8 Ashtabula: 53 (six new cases) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 56 (two new cases) Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 10 Knox: 5 Mahoning: 1 (one new case; first time on the list) Medina: 28 (one new case) Meigs: 4 Mercer: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Pike: 24 (one new case) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 15 (two new cases) Tuscarawas: 15 (two new cases) Van Wert: 3 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 46 (one new case) Wood: 1 Unknown: 1 (one new case) The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Weekly Ohio measles cases by the numbers Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing, as reported by ODH: 310 cases in 25 counties on Nov. 5 296 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 29 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6 Measles kills six in Pennsylvania; infant dies of measles in Wisconsin Pennsylvania confirmed its sixth measles-related death of the year on Nov. 4, while New York announced its first measles death in 30 years on Nov. 2, according to USA TODAY. Wisconsin also reported a grim milestone on Nov. 5, with health officials saying that its first measles death since 1990 was that of an infant. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Measles cases hit 35-year high as US may lose 'eliminated' status The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Falling vaccination rates and the resulting resurgence, however, have raised concerns that the United States could lose its measles elimination status, a designation awarded when a disease has not spread continuously within a country for at least 12 months. The WHO was expected to review the U.S. status on Nov. 10 following the 2025 Texas outbreak that killed three people. Canada already lost its "measles-free" status in November 2025. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

South Carolina ranks second in measles cases as outbreak continues WJCL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 1:10 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 8:26 AM EST Nov 12, 2026 Editorial Standards i Madelyn Cooper Reporter/Producer South Carolina ranks second in measles cases, doctor warns of contagious virus Updated: 8:26 AM EST Nov 12, 2026 Editorial Standards i Madelyn Cooper Reporter/Producer BEAUFORT, S.C. — Measles cases continue to be reported in South Carolina following a major outbreak earlier this year, with the state ranking second nationwide for confirmed cases, according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention. "It's a virus. It is probably one of the most, if not the most contagious disease," said Dr. Kurt Gambla, chief medical officer at Beaufort Memorial. Advertisement Gambla explained that measles can initially resemble the common cold, but a rash typically develops a few days later. "In some rare cases, it can be a fatal disease," Gambla said. The South Carolina Department of Public Health reported 997 cases during the 2026 outbreak. As of the CDC's November 5 update, the state ranks second nationwide for measles cases, with 670 confirmed cases. Gambla noted that more than 4,800 cases have been reported nationwide through October, which is double the number from last year. "We thought that, the outbreak in Spartanburg, we had that kind of resolved by the spring. But there have been some sporadic cases since then," Gambla said. Health experts advise individuals who suspect they may have measles to call ahead before visiting the emergency department to allow staff to prepare. "There are certain precautions for isolation. The only way to confirm it is through a test. Either a swab or blood test or urine test," Gambla said. Vaccination remains the most effective way to protect against measles, Gambla emphasized. "One dose will give 93% immunity. Two doses, 97% immunity," Gambla said. Gambla said treatment focuses on staying hydrated and managing symptoms, as there is no cure for measles and the virus must run its course. Photograph: Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Measles is considered one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine. Photograph: Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images ‘A tremendous step backwards’: US could lose measles elimination status under RFK Jr’s leadership Country is in the middle of worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases nationally The United States could lose its measles elimination status this week, an event likely to cement health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr’s legacy of meddling in vaccine policies amid the worst outbreak of the virus in the US in 35 years. If the US loses its measles-free status, it would join Canada and several European and Asian nations that had eliminated the disease only for it to return. “That is a tremendous step backwards,” said Dr Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center, an attending physician in the division of infectious diseases at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, and a prominent critic of Kennedy. A panel of eight independent experts will consider the epidemiological evidence in Washington DC, part of a group called the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization (WHO). The PAHO director will make the final call. The vaccine limbo in the US is worsening the measles outbreak Read more “Independent of what PAHO says, measles is now endemic in the US. Measles has a foothold in the US,” said Offit. “We’re going to see it this year, we’re going to see it next year,” because the US “critically decreased the percentage” of people vaccinated. The US is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak since 1991 with more than 5,400 cases nationally, according to the Johns Hopkins University International Vaccine Access Center tracker. Just this year, six people have died in Pennsylvania, a child died in New York on election day and an infant died in Wisconsin days later. Nearly every US state has an active outbreak. Measles is considered one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine. The overwhelming majority of Americans vaccinate themselves and their children, but the sheer contagiousness of measles means even small dips in immunity allow it to spread. It kills one to three people per 1,000 people and hospitalizes about one-in-five unvaccinated people who are infected. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is 97% effective against the disease. Although elimination status is a formal public health designation, its loss has real effects on everyday Americans. In just one example, Dr David Margolius, the Cleveland, Ohio, director of public health, is warning people to find proof of their measles vaccination in the event they’re exposed to a measles-positive patient. “Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” said Margolius, who is also a director-at-large of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Without proof, patients face either an immunology blood draw or a 21-day quarantine. Cleveland health authorities have already done a tremendous amount of detective work this year to track down people exposed to measles patients in hospital waiting rooms and elevators. “We reach out to people and for most people, including myself, we have no personal experience with measles,” he said. “They’ve got everything else going on in their life, and now they’re getting this call.” The types of people who contract measles has also changed. In 1963, when the vaccine was first licensed, measles was considered a childhood disease. Most children contracted the disease by the age of five. “Now you’re seeing the epidemiology shift,” said Offit. Two-thirds of people infected with measles in Pennsylvania are adults, a group on which researchers have little information. Mothers have even given birth to babies with measles. “Now, you’re seeing something we just didn’t see at all – congenital measles.” The potential loss of elimination status comes at a tenuous moment for the Trump administration. Republicans just endured a historic drubbing in the midterm elections. Several new Democratic doctors and scientists are slated to come into Congress on promises to hold Kennedy accountable. At the same time, Trump has doubled down on his commitment to vaccine antagonism with the appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff. “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest Maha supporter in the administration,” Kennedy said in a statement about Miller’s appointment. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” Meanwhile, the capacity of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to respond has been significantly hampered by the Trump administration. The agency has lost up to one-third of its staff, Kennedy has interfered in the agency’s reporting of measles deaths and has spread misinformation about the measles vaccines. Even so, Margolius doesn’t lay all the blame at Kennedy’s feet. Vaccine hesitancy was increasing before Trump took office, and pandemic-era disruptions were real. “Some of the narrative has been to pin this on our health secretary, which certainly I think he could do much more to help the situation rather than hurting the situation, but I do think the case count is climbing everywhere,” he said. “This could happen even under a more pro-public health administration.” The second Trump administration also made broad changes that challenge measles elimination globally. Some of Trump’s first acts in 2024 included withdrawal from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Global Vaccine Alliance (GAVI). GAVI provides measles vaccines to nations such as India and Malawi. There are about 95,000 measles deaths globally, according to the World Health Organization, mostly in unvaccinated children under five years old. At home, Republicans also enacted the largest ever federal cut to health insurance, changes expected to result in more than 17 million people losing insurance through 2034. That has challenged people such as Margolius, who struggle to connect people with vaccines when their health insurance coverage is unstable. “Until we can rejoin the WHO and cooperate with other health agencies all over the world ... This will continue,” said Margolius. This article was amended on 11 November 2026. news.source_body_en: The United States is facing its worst measles outbreak since 1991, with over 5,400 cases and six deaths. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is criticized for his vaccine policies, which have led to a significant decrease in vaccination rates. The measles outbreak is highly infectious, with two-thirds of infected individuals being adults, and the potential for congenital measles. The CDC's capacity to respond has been significantly hampered, and the loss of elimination status could have real effects on everyday Americans, requiring proof of vaccination or quarantine.

news.content: News Sports Opinion Business Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals IOWA Polk County confirms case of measles in a child Kyle Werner Des Moines Register Nov. 11, 2026Updated Nov. 12, 2026, 8:16 a.m. CT The Polk County Health Department confirmed a case of measles in a child on Wednesday, Nov. 11. Officials have confirmed 50 cases of measles in Iowa in 2026 as of Nov. 5. Iowa Health and Human Services announced the first measles case of 2026 in July, and confirmed 17 cases at the end of August. In 2025, the state reported just nine cases. Public health officials have evidence that this measles outbreak was spread from person to person. They're encouraging people to identify illnesses, share information and ensure access to vaccination. Places and times infected individuals could have spread measles in Iowa Potential measles exposure locations and times include: Walmart: 1002 National Dr., Ankeny; Thursday, Nov. 5, between 5 and 8 p.m. Hy-Vee: 410 N. Ankeny Blvd., Ankeny; Friday, Nov. 6, between noon and 3 p.m. UnityPoint Clinic Urgent Care: 3625 N. Ankeny Blvd., Ankeny; Sunday, Nov. 8 between 10:10 a.m. and 1:15 p.m. UnityPoint Health – Iowa Methodist Medical Center/Blank Children's Hospital Emergency Department: 1200 Pleasant St., Des Moines (times listed at specific locations below): Iowa Methodist Medical Center/Blank Children's Hospital Emergency Department waiting room between 11:25 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Blank Children’s Hospital Emergency Department between 11:30 a.m. and 5:20 p.m. Hallway from Blank Children’s Emergency Department to Blank Children’s inpatient elevators between 3:15 and 5:25 p.m. Blank Children’s Hospital 4th floor between 3:20 and 10:45 p.m. The Polk County Health Department asks those who visited the locations to take an online survey to track potential exposures. What is measles? What are the symptoms for measles? Measles is a viral illness with symptoms that include fever, cough, red and watery eyes, a runny nose and a rash. Symptoms may appear from 7 to 14 days after contact with someone who is infected and contagious. The virus is spread through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes and breathes and can remain virulent for up to two hours. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 90% of people who come into contact with the virus become infected if they are unvaccinated, making it one of the most contagious diseases known. Additionally, 1 in 5 of those people end up hospitalized, according to the CDC. Measles can cause health complications including ear infections and diarrhea, as well as pneumonia, swelling of the brain and in some cases, death. Children are most at risk for serious complications. In 2025, there was a total of nine measles cases in Iowa and 2,289 across the country, with 243 patients hospitalized and three deaths, according to Iowa HHS. How can I avoid getting measles? Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. The MMR vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella) protects against measles with 97% efficacy, and is typically administered to children as part of the regular vaccine course, with the first dose when the child is 12 to 15 months of age and the second at 4 to 6 years. "With measles continuing to circulate in the region, Iowa HHS anticipates that additional cases may occur, particularly among individuals who are not protected against measles through vaccination or prior infection," HHS said in a news release. The recent increase in measles outbreaks has been attributed to plummeting vaccination rates. What to do if you believe you are infected with measles Those who may have been exposed to the infected individual are asked to monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days and to call their medical provider or the nearest emergency room before arrival and tell them they have been exposed to measles and have symptoms. Register reporters Norah Judson and Lucia Cheng contributed to this report. Kyle Werner is the breaking news and public safety reporter for the Register. Reach him at kwerner@registermedia.com. In 2025, there was a total of nine measles cases in Iowa and 2,289 across the country, with 243 patients hospitalized and three deaths, according to Iowa HHS. How can I avoid getting measles? Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. The MMR vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella) protects against measles with 97% efficacy, and is typically administered to children as part of the regular vaccine course, with the first dose when the child is 12 to 15 months of age and the second at 4 to 6 years. "With measles continuing to circulate in the region, Iowa HHS anticipates that additional cases may occur, particularly among individuals who are not protected against measles through vaccination or prior infection," HHS said in a news release. The recent increase in measles outbreaks has been attributed to plummeting vaccination rates. What to do if you believe you are infected with measles Those who may have been exposed to the infected individual are asked to monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days and to call their medical provider or the nearest emergency room before arrival and tell them they have been exposed to measles and have symptoms. Register reporters Norah Judson and Lucia Cheng contributed to this report. Kyle Werner is the breaking news and public safety reporter for the Register. Reach him at kwerner@registermedia.com. news.content: November 14, 2026 · Beograd Newsroom English €117,62din-0.01%Exchange ratesMarkets ›7°BelgradeForecast › Search⏎ Search Go Politics Sport Economy World Crime Culture Showbiz Lifestyle Technology Science Opinion Weather Exchange rates EnglishNewsroom Theme Politics Sport Economy World Crime Culture Showbiz Lifestyle Technology Science Opinion TRENDING| Veljko Raznatovic to pull children from Titel kindergarten→ Home / Health Health Measles in Serbia: 27 Cases, 18 of Them in Bor Batut reports data through November 8: 22 cases since early October, including a health worker from Pozarevac. What an epidemiologist from Zajecar says. Jelena Đurić·November 10, 2026·2 min read·0 PodeliKopiraj link Illustrative photo for a report on measles in Serbia/ Photo: Pixabay Should you worry about measles? If you have a child who is not vaccinated, there is reason to pay attention. The Institute of Public Health of Serbia “Dr Milan Jovanovic Batut” announced on November 10 that 27 measles cases have been registered in Serbia since the start of the year, through November 8. Most are in Bor. What exactly does Batut say? 22 cases have been registered since the beginning of October. The institute states in its release: “Since the beginning of October, 22 cases of measles have been registered.” Of those, 18 are part of the outbreak reported for the City of Bor on November 4. The other four October cases: two in Belgrade one in Pozarevac one in the area covered by the Public Health Institute in Kosovska Mitrovica The Pozarevac case is a health worker who had contact with a patient from Bor at the Pozarevac General Hospital. Earlier in the year, one case each was recorded in Novi Pazar (April) and Belgrade (May), along with three in the Kosovska Mitrovica institute’s area during August and September. How did the disease spread in Bor? Epidemiologist Svetlana Zivkovic of the “Timok” Public Health Institute in Zajecar described the sequence to RTS. The first to fall ill was an unvaccinated child under one year old, too young for the vaccine. Another child of that age followed, then older unvaccinated children, and finally parents who were either unvaccinated or had not received all doses. Bor currently has 18 confirmed cases, and three more are suspected. Zivkovic said she expected the laboratory results the same day. Why does vaccination matter? Zivkovic says vaccination is the most important measure for stopping the spread of the disease, and that it also protects people who cannot receive it. Coverage is the deciding factor: “It is considered that vaccine coverage should be above 95 percent, and the closer it is to 100 percent, the better the herd immunity,” Zivkovic told RTS. The “Timok” institute and the Children’s Clinic of the Bor Health Center went through vaccination records and compiled lists of eligible children. Invitations are already going out. Zivkovic urges every child who has reached the prescribed age and has no temporary or permanent contraindications to respond. Which complications does Batut list? Young children are the most vulnerable, and pneumonia is the most common complication. Batut says complications are more frequent in children under five, adults over 20 and people with weakened immunity. Figures from the release: middle ear infection: 6 to 8 in 100 patients pneumonia: 1 to 6 in 100 patients encephalitis: 1 to 2 in 1,000 patients There is also a rare, severe late complication, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which appears years after infection. The younger the patient at the time of illness, the higher the risk. What can parents of infants do? The virus spreads easily through the air, so the epidemiologist has specific advice for those whose children are too young to be vaccinated: “I advise parents to avoid crowds, gatherings and long stays in enclosed spaces with very small children, those under one year old,” Zivkovic said.
