news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Preventable Systems Failures Driven by Supply Gaps Trigger Bangladesh Measles Resurgence by November 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Preventable Systems Failures Driven by Supply Gaps Trigger Bangladesh Measles Resurgence Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A perspective analysis published in Discover Public Health reports that Bangladesh has confronted its most severe measles outbreak in decades during 2026, documenting more than 50,500 suspected cases and at least 415 confirmed or suspected measles-related deaths between mid-March and mid-May. The analysis, authored by Md. Abdus Salam, characterizes this widespread public health crisis not as an unavoidable biological occurrence, but as a preventable systems failure that reversed years of hard-won progress toward disease elimination. Historically recognized as an international benchmark for immunization programming in resource-constrained environments, the country experienced an erosion of protective herd immunity when systemic administrative disruptions, nationwide vaccine supply shortages, and prolonged intervals between supplemental vaccination campaigns converged to expose expanding cohorts of unprotected children. The historical trajectory of measles control in Bangladesh highlights the scale of the recent setback. In the early 2000s, measles persisted as a major cause of pediatric mortality across the country, with national coverage for the first dose of measles-containing vaccine stagnating at or below 75 percent and zero administrative districts reaching the 95 percent coverage threshold necessary to interrupt transmission. Sustained national investments in the Expanded Programme on Immunization, combined with integrated child health days, routine vitamin A distribution, and recurring nationwide supplementary immunization activities, gradually lifted first-dose administrative coverage from approximately 74 to 89 percent in 2000 to between 94 and 118 percent by 2016. In parallel, the introduction of a routine second measles-containing vaccine dose in 2012 expanded second-dose coverage from roughly one-third of eligible children to more than 90 percent by the mid-2010s, driving laboratory-confirmed measles incidence down by more than 80 percent from approximately 40 cases per million population to 6 per million. Discover more Health health Get Health Tips Despite these extensive historical gains, national surveillance data compiled by domestic health agencies and international monitoring bodies revealed an underlying accumulation of susceptible individuals starting after 2019. National coverage estimates for both the first and second doses of the combined measles-rubella vaccine plateaued and subsequently exhibited modest declines. First-dose coverage slipped from approximately 88 to 89 percent down to 86 percent, while second-dose coverage dropped from roughly 89 percent to 80.7 percent by the 2023 to 2024 monitoring period, leaving an estimated 20 million children partially or entirely unprotected against infection. Compounding these gradual routine reductions, Bangladesh failed to conduct any nationwide measles-rubella supplementary immunization activities following its 2020 campaign, departing from its historical schedule of four-yearly catch-up exercises due to operational disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent domestic political instability. Discover more Check Symptoms public health Public Health Track Outbreaks The vulnerability deepened considerably between 2024 and 2025 following a nationwide stockout of the measles-rubella vaccine, which the perspective links to procedural shifts in procurement arrangements and administrative delays that accompanied a broader political transition. A planned nationwide supplementary campaign originally scheduled for 2024 was postponed, remained unimplemented throughout 2025, and was ultimately cancelled altogether. While international evaluations by the World Health Organization and UNICEF recorded routine coverage figures of 97 percent for the first dose and 93 percent for the second dose in 2023, certain internal national reports cited an acute drop to approximately 56 to 59 percent coverage by 2025. Although the author notes that discrepancies between administrative datasets and independent field surveys preclude an absolute causal determination, the accumulated evidence indicates that these procurement disruptions expanded the pool of susceptible hosts precisely when routine delivery systems were operating under strain. When transmission expanded rapidly in early 2026, the infectious pathogen exploited these accumulated immunity gaps with severe clinical consequences. The National International Health Regulations Focal Point formally notified the World Health Organization of an accelerating nationwide increase in measles cases on April 4, 2026. Directorate General of Health Services data recorded 50,500 suspected cases and 415 deaths by May 11, reflecting a crude reported death-to-suspected-case ratio of approximately 0.82 percent. Epidemiological tracking between April 22 and May 4 documented cumulative suspected cases surging from 27,164 to 41,793, laboratory-confirmed infections rising from 3,934 to 5,467, and reported deaths increasing from 190 to 311. Approximately 79 to 80 percent of all reported infections occurred among children under five years of age, with 66 percent concentrated in children under two years and roughly one-third occurring in infants younger than nine months who were not yet eligible for standard routine measles immunization. The spatial distribution of cases revealed severe localized burdens, with the outbreak reaching 58 of Bangladesh’s 64 administrative districts across all eight divisions while concentrating heavily within specific urban slums, peripheral settlements, and humanitarian zones. In the capital division of Dhaka alone, situation reports documented more than 18,000 to 19,000 cases, heavily clustering within densely populated informal settlements including Demra, Jatrabari, Kamrangirchar, Korail, Mirpur, and Tejgaon. Within these crowded urban environments, high population density, economic precarity, and geographic mobility presented substantial barriers to routine healthcare delivery. Outside municipal centers, field monitoring in Gopalganj identified zero-dose children among highly mobile floating families who had been bypassed by both standard clinic-based schedules and targeted door-to-door immunization initiatives. Humanitarian settings presented another critical vulnerability during the 2026 resurgence, particularly within the congested Rohingya refugee camps established across Cox’s Bazar. Transmission within the camp complex escalated from 19 suspected cases in January to 199 in February, reaching 76 suspected cases with 8 confirmed infections by March. By mid-May, diagnostic testing confirmed 60 cases alongside 239 suspected cases and 5 attributable deaths, expanding to a cumulative total of 595 suspected cases and 60 laboratory-confirmed cases by May 20. The extreme transmissibility of the measles virus within these humanitarian enclaves was exacerbated by constrained baseline access to clinical services, widespread dependence on external humanitarian assistance, high rates of background malnutrition, and persistent cohorts of completely unvaccinated zero-dose infants residing in close quarters. The perspective emphasizes that the clinical severity of the outbreak was compounded by frequent secondary complications, most notably acute pneumonia, persistent diarrhea, and severe metabolic wasting linked directly to pre-existing childhood undernutrition and vitamin A deficiencies. Surging patient volumes placed severe operational strain on secondary and tertiary clinical centers, with daily hospital admissions frequently surpassing 1,200 to 1,300 patients. This influx rapidly overwhelmed pediatric wards and exposed structural deficits in facility-based isolation units, available health personnel, and laboratory diagnostic reagents. Clinical observations indicated that severe disease and fatal outcomes remained heavily concentrated among under-vaccinated or unvaccinated young children, demonstrating how nutritional deficits and immunization lapses synergistically worsen pediatric outcomes during large-scale community transmission. Bangladesh’s domestic outbreak mirrors a broader post-pandemic deterioration of measles control observed internationally. According to World Health Organization global monitoring figures, 59 countries experienced large or disruptive measles outbreaks in 2024—nearly three times the total recorded in 2021—including several jurisdictions that had previously attained verified elimination status. Worldwide, estimated coverage for the first vaccine dose reached approximately 84 to 86 percent in 2024, with second-dose uptake estimated at 76 percent, leaving global coverage well beneath the 95 percent threshold necessary to maintain community herd protection. Regionally, concurrent case increases and localized outbreaks were documented across India, Nepal, Thailand, and the Maldives, prompting public health authorities in neighboring Myanmar to reinforce cross-border surveillance and clinical preparedness along its frontier to mitigate potential cross-border transmission. In response to the crisis, the Government of Bangladesh joined with international partners, including the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and Gavi, to mount an emergency response campaign starting on April 5, 2026. Initially deployed across 30 high-risk upazilas in 18 districts, the intervention expanded into four city corporations before rolling out nationwide on April 20, strategically lowering the eligibility age to six months to shield vulnerable infants. Responders distributed more than 20 million vaccine doses, trained over 26,000 frontline health workers, and integrated vitamin A supplementation into clinical case management. Although administrative tracking recorded more than 18.3 million children vaccinated by May 19—surpassing initial national targets—an independent assessment published by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies on May 5 reported national administrative coverage at only 60.57 percent, noting that multiple districts had reached fewer than half of their target populations while active transmission continued. Concluding his evaluation, Salam argues that the 2026 epidemic serves as a clear indicator of structural fragility in primary health systems, illustrating that high national coverage metrics often obscure dangerous localized pockets of susceptibility. Rebuilding long-term resilience will require immediate stabilization of the national vaccine pipeline through secured buffer inventories, independent supplier verification mechanisms, and statutory protections that isolate essential medicine procurement from administrative or political transitions. Over the longer horizon, the perspective calls for institutionalizing regular supplementary catch-up campaigns, modernizing disease surveillance with real-time laboratory reporting, and prioritizing micro-planning in urban informal settlements and humanitarian camps to ensure sustained protection for marginalized and zero-dose populations before explosive outbreaks can emerge. Responders distributed more than 20 million vaccine doses, trained over 26,000 frontline health workers, and integrated vitamin A supplementation into clinical case management. Although administrative tracking recorded more than 18.3 million children vaccinated by May 19—surpassing initial national targets—an independent assessment published by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies on May 5 reported national administrative coverage at only 60.57 percent, noting that multiple districts had reached fewer than half of their target populations while active transmission continued. Concluding his evaluation, Salam argues that the 2026 epidemic serves as a clear indicator of structural fragility in primary health systems, illustrating that high national coverage metrics often obscure dangerous localized pockets of susceptibility. Rebuilding long-term resilience will require immediate stabilization of the national vaccine pipeline through secured buffer inventories, independent supplier verification mechanisms, and statutory protections that isolate essential medicine procurement from administrative or political transitions. Over the longer horizon, the perspective calls for institutionalizing regular supplementary catch-up campaigns, modernizing disease surveillance with real-time laboratory reporting, and prioritizing micro-planning in urban informal settlements and humanitarian camps to ensure sustained protection for marginalized and zero-dose populations before explosive outbreaks can emerge. Vermont health officials say they have confirmed connected cases of measles in Orleans County. They say the risk to the general public remains low, but that an investigation is ongoing. Vermont Health Commissioner Rick Hildebrant said the number of cases remained “less than five” for now, but characterized the situation as “evolving.” “We have the risk of seeing person-to-person transmission within the state of Vermont. We have not seen that yet. But I am fearful that we might,” he said in an interview Tuesday. Hildebrant said that the disease was believed to have been contracted when people traveled out-of-state but within the country. Measles cases have been occurring in Vermont more frequently in recent years as vaccination rates wane and the disease sees a resurgence nationwide. Hildebrant noted that this Vermont news had arrived in the same week as the Pan American Health Organization, an international public health agency, is expected to evaluate whether the U.S. should retain its measles elimination status. “That should never have happened. It shouldn't be happening. We are seeing deaths in America that we should not see,” the health commissioner said. Health officials in Vermont last detected a case of measles this February. The state also reported two cases in both 2025 and 2024. In the decade prior, Vermont had confirmed just one case in 2011 and one in 2018. The disease is highly contagious and spreads through the air. It can lead to dangerous and even fatal complications, like brain swelling and pneumonia, particularly in young children and those who aren’t vaccinated. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people who get measles are hospitalized, according to the CDC. There is no cure for measles, but research shows the measles, mumps, and rubella — or MMR — vaccine is extremely effective at preventing the disease. “A single shot of MMR protects 93% against measles, and two is 97%. So while yes, general infection control practices are warranted, the reality is, given how contagious this illness is, that's not going to do it,” Hildebrant said. “You need to get vaccinated.” Measles shots are free in Vermont, even if someone is uninsured. The health department has published a list of resources to help Vermonters figure out if they’ve been immunized, and how to get vaccinated if they want to. surging in the U.S. — and outbreaks can cost millions Published Wed, Nov 11 20267:00 AM ESTUpdated Wed, Nov 11 202610:14 AM EST Annika Kim Constantino@annikakimc WATCH LIVE ShareShare Article via FacebookShare Article via TwitterShare Article via LinkedInShare Article via Email 0 seconds of 0 secondsVolume 90% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Seek %0-9 1x1.5x2x Listen8min Live 00:00 00:00 08:27 2x1.5x1x Key Points The return of measles in the U.S. can carry a huge financial burden on the U.S. healthcare system. A new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates that the 2025 measles outbreak in the U.S. — which involved roughly 2,300 confirmed cases nationwide — carried an economic cost of more than $37 million. Those costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources spent investigating and containing outbreaks and wages lost when people have to miss work. Measles outbreaks aren’t just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely. The U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year. More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin. Based on this year’s case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The tool also estimates that 2025 measles outbreaks in the U.S. — which involved 2,289 confirmed cases nationwide – carried an economic cost of more than $37 million. The costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources health departments spend investigating and containing outbreaks, as well as wages lost when people have to miss work. The tool uses more recent, state-specific cost and financing data than an initial study by the researchers, which relied on historical outbreak costs. The estimates from the tool are not a definitive accounting of what the outbreaks actually cost. But it illustrates the hefty bill tied to the spread of a disease that can be prevented through vaccination, and the potential economic consequences of falling childhood immunization rates. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation’s public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. “We’re starting to see a whole bunch of people who decided not to get vaccinated as kids or have never gotten exposed to measles because they benefited from herd immunity, who now make it into adulthood and risk potentially getting quite seriously ill and requiring very significant medical expenses, or dying at the hospital,” Bryan Patenaude, a health economist at the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who helped develop the tool, said in an interview. The costs of containing measles Measles outbreaks can trigger a costly public health response, even when many people who are exposed never become sick. When a case is identified, public health officials must investigate the infection, identify and notify people who may have been exposed, coordinate with hospitals and schools, and sometimes organize vaccination campaigns to prevent further spread. Those efforts can divert staff and resources from other public health priorities. watch now VIDEO3:0303:03 What the measles outbreak signals for the U.S. Health and Science Costs could differ heavily depending on the state. Johns Hopkins’ data includes national averages alongside state-specific inputs, including inpatient hospital costs and wages from government data or trusted health policy sources. In New York, for example, the average inpatient hospital stay is roughly $4,200 a day, while the minimum wage is $16 per hour. The tool estimates that the 48 cases reported by New York in 2025 carried an estimated $1.1 million in costs, including nearly $749,000 in public health responses, $333,000 in productivity losses and roughly $24,500 in direct medical expenses. Meanwhile, the 803 cases in Texas, the epicenter of the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 2025, carried estimated costs of nearly $13 million, according to the tool. That includes $9 million in public health costs, $4 million in productivity losses and around $288,000 in direct medical expenses. The tool builds on a study published by Patenaude and other researchers in August, which examined the costs of measles outbreaks in the U.S. The researchers reviewed published studies and government reports to compile historical estimates of medical expenses and public health response costs across 18 states. The paper estimated that outbreaks carried a historical average cost of nearly $59,000 per case, just from the public health response. The researchers also estimated how costs scale with outbreak size, separating fixed up-front response expenses from the additional costs associated with each new case. “A lot of this is incurred up front, and that’s because of the human labor that’s involved in contact tracing and all of the different actors that sort of need to be mobilized to deal with the fact that there’s an outbreak,” Patenaude told CNBC. “It’s a largely labor-driven cost.” That model estimated roughly $298,000 in fixed costs and about $16,300 for each additional case. But it relied on historical data, including a particularly large 2019 outbreak in New York City, where contact-tracing labor costs were high. The researchers also excluded productivity losses from that model because most of the historical studies they reviewed did not consistently account for them. The costs of lost productivity A medical assistant gives a measles, mumps and rubella, vaccination to a young person at the pediatric office of Dr. Gary M. Kramer in Coral Gables, Florida, Aug. 13, 2026. Joe Raedle | Getty Images The economic burden of measles extends beyond the costs of treating infected patients and organizing a public health response. People who are exposed to measles may have to quarantine, even if they never develop symptoms. Parents can also be forced to miss work to care for sick or exposed children, while workers who contract the disease may lose wages during their recovery. A 2025 study by Joey Mattingly, a pharmacist and health economist at the University of Utah, used published epidemiological and cost data to model the potential economic burden of a hypothetical 1,500-case outbreak. His analysis included direct medical expenses, public health spending and lost productivity, and examined how the estimates changed under different assumptions, including hospitalization rates. The study estimated that the hypothetical outbreak could cost about $90 million, including roughly $26 million in productivity losses. The economic ripple effects of a case Those indirect costs can add up quickly because measles is highly contagious and a single infected person can expose dozens of others. Those contacts may need to quarantine or miss work while health officials determine whether they have been infected, creating costs even when they never develop the disease. Mattingly estimated that each person who is quarantined could amount to roughly $300 in lost productivity alone. If a single measles case exposes 40 to 50 people who then need to quarantine, that could translate into an estimated $12,000 to $15,000 in lost productivity, even if none of those contacts become sick. MMR vaccine administer prep is pictured during a drive at the City of Lubbock Health Department in Texas, Feb. 27, 2025. Annie Rice | Reuters That ripple effect is one reason Mattingly argues that the economic costs of outbreaks can quickly outweigh the investment required to vaccinate people against measles. “Even if you don’t get the infection, the contact costs you,” he said. “And so it’s just showing that there’s this multiplication or exponential growth on the economic side that happens.” The financial burden can also fall unevenly across communities. While the costs of responding to an outbreak may be shared among local, state and federal agencies, Mattingly said the impact is often felt directly by local health departments. “It’s not like your health department is sitting around waiting for measles outbreaks,” he said. “They’re working, doing all these other things, and imagine having to just drop what you’re doing because there’s been a huge outbreak in the community.” Patenaude said the findings could help state and local health departments better anticipate the resources needed to contain outbreaks — particularly as measles cases continue to rise. “It’s not super expensive to treat and deal with a single case of measles compared to a single case of cancer,” he said. “But if you have these outbreaks popping up and you’re having to constantly divert resources that could be spent elsewhere by state and local health departments on measles, then you’re going to wind up spending a lot of money very quickly.” Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news. 00:00 00:00 08:27 2x1.5x1x Key Points The return of measles in the U.S. can carry a huge financial burden on the U.S. healthcare system. A new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates that the 2025 measles outbreak in the U.S. — which involved roughly 2,300 confirmed cases nationwide — carried an economic cost of more than $37 million. Those costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources spent investigating and containing outbreaks and wages lost when people have to miss work. Measles outbreaks aren’t just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely. The U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year. More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin. Based on this year’s case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The tool also estimates that 2025 measles outbreaks in the U.S. — which involved 2,289 confirmed cases nationwide – carried an economic cost of more than $37 million. The costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources health departments spend investigating and containing outbreaks, as well as wages lost when people have to miss work. The tool uses more recent, state-specific cost and financing data than an initial study by the researchers, which relied on historical outbreak costs. The estimates from the tool are not a definitive accounting of what the outbreaks actually cost. But it illustrates the hefty bill tied to the spread of a disease that can be prevented through vaccination, and the potential economic consequences of falling childhood immunization rates. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation’s public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. “We’re starting to see a whole bunch of people who decided not to get vaccinated as kids or have never gotten exposed to measles because they benefited from herd immunity, who now make it into adulthood and risk potentially getting quite seriously ill and requiring very significant medical expenses, or dying at the hospital,” Bryan Patenaude, a health economist at the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who helped develop the tool, said in an interview. The costs of containing measles Measles outbreaks can trigger a costly public health response, even when many people who are exposed never become sick. When a case is identified, public health officials must investigate the infection, identify and notify people who may have been exposed, coordinate with hospitals and schools, and sometimes organize vaccination campaigns to prevent further spread. Those efforts can divert staff and resources from other public health priorities. watch now VIDEO3:0303:03 What the measles outbreak signals for the U.S. Health and Science Costs could differ heavily depending on the state. Johns Hopkins’ data includes national averages alongside state-specific inputs, including inpatient hospital costs and wages from government data or trusted health policy sources. In New York, for example, the average inpatient hospital stay is roughly $4,200 a day, while the minimum wage is $16 per hour. The tool estimates that the 48 cases reported by New York in 2025 carried an estimated $1.1 million in costs, including nearly $749,000 in public health responses, $333,000 in productivity losses and roughly $24,500 in direct medical expenses. Meanwhile, the 803 cases in Texas, the epicenter of the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 2025, carried estimated costs of nearly $13 million, according to the tool. That includes $9 million in public health costs, $4 million in productivity losses and around $288,000 in direct medical expenses. The tool builds on a study published by Patenaude and other researchers in August, which examined the costs of measles outbreaks in the U.S. The researchers reviewed published studies and government reports to compile historical estimates of medical expenses and public health response costs across 18 states. The paper estimated that outbreaks carried a historical average cost of nearly $59,000 per case, just from the public health response. The researchers also estimated how costs scale with outbreak size, separating fixed up-front response expenses from the additional costs associated with each new case. “A lot of this is incurred up front, and that’s because of the human labor that’s involved in contact tracing and all of the different actors that sort of need to be mobilized to deal with the fact that there’s an outbreak,” Patenaude told CNBC. “It’s a largely labor-driven cost.” That model estimated roughly $298,000 in fixed costs and about $16,300 for each additional case. But it relied on historical data, including a particularly large 2019 outbreak in New York City, where contact-tracing labor costs were high. The researchers also excluded productivity losses from that model because most of the historical studies they reviewed did not consistently account for them. The costs of lost productivity A medical assistant gives a measles, mumps and rubella, vaccination to a young person at the pediatric office of Dr. Gary M. Kramer in Coral Gables, Florida, Aug. 13, 2026. Joe Raedle | Getty Images The economic burden of measles extends beyond the costs of treating infected patients and organizing a public health response. People who are exposed to measles may have to quarantine, even if they never develop symptoms. Parents can also be forced to miss work to care for sick or exposed children, while workers who contract the disease may lose wages during their recovery. A 2025 study by Joey Mattingly, a pharmacist and health economist at the University of Utah, used published epidemiological and cost data to model the potential economic burden of a hypothetical 1,500-case outbreak. His analysis included direct medical expenses, public health spending and lost productivity, and examined how the estimates changed under different assumptions, including hospitalization rates. The study estimated that the hypothetical outbreak could cost about $90 million, including roughly $26 million in productivity losses. The economic ripple effects of a case Those indirect costs can add up quickly because measles is highly contagious and a single infected person can expose dozens of others. Those contacts may need to quarantine or miss work while health officials determine whether they have been infected, creating costs even when they never develop the disease. Mattingly estimated that each person who is quarantined could amount to roughly $300 in lost productivity alone. If a single measles case exposes 40 to 50 people who then need to quarantine, that could translate into an estimated $12,000 to $15,000 in lost productivity, even if none of those contacts become sick. MMR vaccine administer prep is pictured during a drive at the City of Lubbock Health Department in Texas, Feb. 27, 2025. Annie Rice | Reuters That ripple effect is one reason Mattingly argues that the economic costs of outbreaks can quickly outweigh the investment required to vaccinate people against measles. “Even if you don’t get the infection, the contact costs you,” he said. “And so it’s just showing that there’s this multiplication or exponential growth on the economic side that happens.” The financial burden can also fall unevenly across communities. While the costs of responding to an outbreak may be shared among local, state and federal agencies, Mattingly said the impact is often felt directly by local health departments. “It’s not like your health department is sitting around waiting for measles outbreaks,” he said. “They’re working, doing all these other things, and imagine having to just drop what you’re doing because there’s been a huge outbreak in the community.” Patenaude said the findings could help state and local health departments better anticipate the resources needed to contain outbreaks — particularly as measles cases continue to rise. “It’s not super expensive to treat and deal with a single case of measles compared to a single case of cancer,” he said. “But if you have these outbreaks popping up and you’re having to constantly divert resources that could be spent elsewhere by state and local health departments on measles, then you’re going to wind up spending a lot of money very quickly.” Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news. news.content_title: An Investigational Drug to Tackle Measles Outbreaks
news.content: SHELTON, CT / ACCESS Newswire / November 10, 2026 / NanoViricides, Inc., a publicly traded company (NYSE American: NNVC ) (the “Company”), and a clinical stage, leading global pioneer in the development of broad-spectrum antivirals based on host-mimetic nanomedicine technology that viruses cannot escape, announces that it is advancing its Measles drug development program towards clinical trials. There have been three deaths in children due to Measles in the USA in the last ten days, one each in the states of New York, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin i . This condition should be unacceptable in the USA because there is already a drug against Measles that has shown effectiveness in a humanized animal model of Measles, that has gone through extensive studies including Phase I human safety study, and that is already in two Phase II clinical trials for other viral infections. This investigational drug is NV-387, a novel, revolutionary broad-spectrum, antiviral drug developed by the Company. This drug has completed a juvenile animal model study as well. NV-387 is not yet FDA-approved or commercially available for treating Measles or any other viral disease. However, we believe the drug NV-387 now has sufficient data available to enable use under the US FDA physician-initiated investigational new drug application mechanism that is designed for use of experimental drugs for specific severe cases of disease, such as Measles. The Company continues to develop this drug in the regulatory pathways. There were 5,164 confirmed Measles cases within the USA (excluding international visitors) as of November 5, 2026, reported in 47 jurisdictions, with 4% of these being breakthrough cases in vaccinated individuals, and remaining 96% in unvaccinated individuals. 562 (11%) of the cases were hospitalized, and 4 confirmed Measles-caused deaths were recorded. A few additional deaths in Measles cases that are under CDC review have also occurred. Majority of hospitalizations occurred in children under 5 years of age. Only 4 states, namely Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, and Nevada have not reported a Measles case in 2026, according to the CDC ii . These data indicate that Measles in the USA is continuing to expand in 2026. At this point, loss of the Measles elimination status achieved by the USA in 2000 as the very first country to achieve this status would be merely symbolic, emphasizing that Measles is a globally endemic virus with a very high potential for creating a contagion. Vaccines, even though effective, are inadequate as the only response to such a disease as Measles, and drugs to treat Measles infections are sorely needed. Of note, the D8 genotype of the Measles virus dominates in 2026 US cases iii whereas the Measles vaccine is based on the A genotype. NV-387, the Company’s revolutionary clinical stage broad-spectrum antiviral drug is currently in a Phase II clinical trials as an oral treatment for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The same drug, NV-387, formulated as the same oral gummies formulation is also in a Phase II clinical trial for the treatment of Mpox (Monkeypox) in DRC in a different province. This very same drug has demonstrated remarkable antiviral activity against the Measles virus in a humanized hCD150+, IfnAR-/- mouse model of Measles virus infection and disease. The Company has also completed a repeat-dose juvenile mouse model toxicity study in which 4-day old mouse pups were dosed with repeated doses of NV-387 oral gummies formulation to evaluate the safety and tolerability of the drug and drug product in the context of the use of the drug in children. Under the conditions of this Juvenile Mouse Model study, the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) was determined to be 1,230 mg/kg per dose administered three times daily, or 3,690 mg/kg/day, or a total cumulative drug exposure of 44,280 mg/kg over the 12 day dosing period. This was actually the highest dose level tested. Therefore, a Maximum Tolerable Dose (MTD) could not be estimated iv . Further, there was no mortality, systemic toxicity, treatment-related clinical observations, adverse effects on body weight gain, alterations in cardiovascular parameters, changes in clinical pathology, or treatment-related gross or microscopic pathological findings observed in either sex. According to established guidelines for juvenile animal model data extrapolation, a drug evaluated for safety toxicology in 4 day mouse pups supports clinical pediatric study in infants as young as 1 month v , under an appropriate regulatory study. Cases of Measles have been rising globally for different reasons. The measles outbreak in Bangladesh has continued to proliferate, claiming 24,073 lab-confirmed cases with 105 fatalities in lab-confirmed cases from 15 March to 10 November, 2026. During this period, a total of 207,428 patients with suspected measles were hospitalized and 1,263 persons, mostly children, have died of suspected measles, while 1,318 new suspected measles cases with at least 6 more child deaths were reported in just the last 24 hours in Bangladesh vi . The measles outbreak in Bangladesh has continued despite aggressive vaccination campaign that was undertaken since April-May 2026. There is currently no approved drug for measles. Vaccine does not help a patient already infected with the measles virus. Vaccinating already measles-exposed persons to avoid disease spread is attempted yet measles has continued to spread in the USA. Thus an effective treatment for Measles is an unmet medical need. NV-387 is the only drug candidate to our knowledge that has demonstrated strong in vivo activity against lethal infection with the Measles virus in a humanized animal model study, supporting its clinical regulatory development for treatment of Measles. NanoViricides is currently developing a Phase II clinical trial protocol for evaluating NV-387 as a treatment for measles. A draft is being circulated. The Company intends to bring this protocol under the purview of the US FDA in an IND process. Therefore, this work is expected to take some time. NV-387 has been granted a “Rare Pediatric Disease Drug” (RPDD) Designation by the US FDA Office of Orphan Products Development (OOPD). This RPDD designation enables that a Priority Review Voucher (PRV) can be issued to the Company upon a successful Marketing Application (i.e. New Drug Application) for the use of NV-387 as a treatment for Measles, provided all of the required conditions are met. The Company can use the PRV, if granted, to reduce review times on another of its drug applications. A PRV can be sold to another Pharma Company for accelerating their drug program as well, which provides a high value to the purchaser. PRVs have been sold for as much as $200 Million vii . “The Rare Pediatric Disease Drug Designation and associated Priority Review Voucher that can be issued make a strong business case for development of NV-387 as a drug for the treatment of Measles,” said Anil R. Diwan, PhD., adding, “NV-387, as an effective drug would be an important tool to fight Measles resurgence in the USA and worldwide, when approved.” FDA has granted both ODD and RPDD for NV-387 as a Treatment of Measles. In addition to the PRV eligibility provided by the RPDD for NV-387 as a treatment of Measles, the Orphan Drug Designation qualifies NanoViricides for incentives including: Tax credits for qualified clinical trials; Exemption from certain user fees; Potential seven years of market exclusivity after approval; according to the US FDA viii . Measles continues to be a rare disease in the USA, with annual incidence rates well below 200,000 cases. Measles primarily affects children. These facts have qualified NV-387 for Measles Treatment for an Orphan Drug Designation, and also for a Rare Pediatric Disease Drug Designation. In a rare disease scenario, commercial revenue from the drug may be slow and small. The PRV is designed to incentivize drug development for rare pediatric diseases by providing additional business value. Measles cases are rising across the Western world including several European countries and the UK, as well as the USA and Canada. Additionally Mexico and several other Central and South American countries have also been suffering from rising Measles outbreaks. Measles is endemic globally; many countries that had achieved an elimination status for Measles have by now lost this status, due to severe outbreaks over the last three years ix . Measles is a highly contagious disease, and spreads via virus particles in bodily fluids upon close contact. A population vaccination rate of at least 95% is required to provide “herd immunity” and block community spread. Such a high rate is difficult to maintain for several reasons. Firstly, vaccine hesitancy is rising globally. Secondly, persons with co-morbidities such as immune-compromise status, diabetes, obesity, etc. do not respond fully to any vaccination. Even if vaccinated, such a person can still get Measles, suffering from possibly a mild disease, but will still be contagious and spread Measles. Additionally, the Measles virus continues to change, with the B and D genotypes in circulation currently, while the vaccines in use are still the ones developed for the A genotype in the 1960’s. Further, very high rates of infections in vaccinated subjects (called “breakthrough cases”), from 14% to 57%, have occurred in some outbreaks x suggesting that resistant virus strains may have been involved. Therefore, an effective treatment for Measles is an unmet medical need, that is expected to become even more important in the near future than it is today. Only an effective treatment can help the patient and can avoid the potential severe disease scenarios such as encephalitis, neurological disabilities, and potential fatalities as well as immune amnesia that can result from severe disease. Quicker recovery of a patient means less chances for spread and thus better ability to control an outbreak. This would require an effective treatment. NV-387 is an extremely broad-spectrum antiviral drug that has demonstrated strong effectiveness in relevant animal models of multiple human viral infections. These include RSV, COVID, Influenza, Mpox, Smallpox, and Measles. ABOUT NANOVIRICIDES NanoViricides, Inc. (the “Company”) ( www.nanoviricides.com ) is a publicly traded (NYSE-American, stock symbol NNVC) clinical stage company that is creating special purpose nanomaterials for antiviral therapy. The Company’s novel nanoviricide TM class of drug candidates and the nanoviricide TM technology are based on intellectual property, technology and proprietary know-how of TheraCour Pharma, Inc. The Company has a Memorandum of Understanding with TheraCour for the development of drugs based on these technologies for all antiviral infections. The MoU does not include cancer and similar diseases that may have viral origin but require different kinds of treatments. news.content_original: SHELTON, CT / ACCESS Newswire / November 10, 2026 / NanoViricides, Inc., a publicly traded company (NYSE American: NNVC ) (the “Company”), and a clinical stage, leading global pioneer in the development of broad-spectrum antivirals based on host-mimetic nanomedicine technology that viruses cannot escape, announces that it is advancing its Measles drug development program towards clinical trials. There have been three deaths in children due to Measles in the USA in the last ten days, one each in the states of New York, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin i . This condition should be unacceptable in the USA because there is already a drug against Measles that has shown effectiveness in a humanized animal model of Measles, that has gone through extensive studies including Phase I human safety study, and that is already in two Phase II clinical trials for other viral infections. This investigational drug is NV-387, a novel, revolutionary broad-spectrum, antiviral drug developed by the Company. This drug has completed a juvenile animal model study as well. NV-387 is not yet FDA-approved or commercially available for treating Measles or any other viral disease. However, we believe the drug NV-387 now has sufficient data available to enable use under the US FDA physician-initiated investigational new drug application mechanism that is designed for use of experimental drugs for specific severe cases of disease, such as Measles. The Company continues to develop this drug in the regulatory pathways. There were 5,164 confirmed Measles cases within the USA (excluding international visitors) as of November 5, 2026, reported in 47 jurisdictions, with 4% of these being breakthrough cases in vaccinated individuals, and remaining 96% in unvaccinated individuals. 562 (11%) of the cases were hospitalized, and 4 confirmed Measles-caused deaths were recorded. A few additional deaths in Measles cases that are under CDC review have also occurred. Majority of hospitalizations occurred in children under 5 years of age. Only 4 states, namely Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, and Nevada have not reported a Measles case in 2026, according to the CDC ii . These data indicate that Measles in the USA is continuing to expand in 2026. At this point, loss of the Measles elimination status achieved by the USA in 2000 as the very first country to achieve this status would be merely symbolic, emphasizing that Measles is a globally endemic virus with a very high potential for creating a contagion. Vaccines, even though effective, are inadequate as the only response to such a disease as Measles, and drugs to treat Measles infections are sorely needed. Of note, the D8 genotype of the Measles virus dominates in 2026 US cases iii whereas the Measles vaccine is based on the A genotype. NV-387, the Company’s revolutionary clinical stage broad-spectrum antiviral drug is currently in a Phase II clinical trials as an oral treatment for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The same drug, NV-387, formulated as the same oral gummies formulation is also in a Phase II clinical trial for the treatment of Mpox (Monkeypox) in DRC in a different province. This very same drug has demonstrated remarkable antiviral activity against the Measles virus in a humanized hCD150+, IfnAR-/- mouse model of Measles virus infection and disease. The Company has also completed a repeat-dose juvenile mouse model toxicity study in which 4-day old mouse pups were dosed with repeated doses of NV-387 oral gummies formulation to evaluate the safety and tolerability of the drug and drug product in the context of the use of the drug in children. Under the conditions of this Juvenile Mouse Model study, the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) was determined to be 1,230 mg/kg per dose administered three times daily, or 3,690 mg/kg/day, or a total cumulative drug exposure of 44,280 mg/kg over the 12 day dosing period. This was actually the highest dose level tested. Therefore, a Maximum Tolerable Dose (MTD) could not be estimated iv . Further, there was no mortality, systemic toxicity, treatment-related clinical observations, adverse effects on body weight gain, alterations in cardiovascular parameters, changes in clinical pathology, or treatment-related gross or microscopic pathological findings observed in either sex. According to established guidelines for juvenile animal model data extrapolation, a drug evaluated for safety toxicology in 4 day mouse pups supports clinical pediatric study in infants as young as 1 month v , under an appropriate regulatory study. Cases of Measles have been rising globally for different reasons. The measles outbreak in Bangladesh has continued to proliferate, claiming 24,073 lab-confirmed cases with 105 fatalities in lab-confirmed cases from 15 March to 10 November, 2026. During this period, a total of 207,428 patients with suspected measles were hospitalized and 1,263 persons, mostly children, have died of suspected measles, while 1,318 new suspected measles cases with at least 6 more child deaths were reported in just the last 24 hours in Bangladesh vi . The measles outbreak in Bangladesh has continued despite aggressive vaccination campaign that was undertaken since April-May 2026. There is currently no approved drug for measles. Vaccine does not help a patient already infected with the measles virus. Vaccinating already measles-exposed persons to avoid disease spread is attempted yet measles has continued to spread in the USA. Thus an effective treatment for Measles is an unmet medical need. NV-387 is the only drug candidate to our knowledge that has demonstrated strong in vivo activity against lethal infection with the Measles virus in a humanized animal model study, supporting its clinical regulatory development for treatment of Measles. The PRV is designed to incentivize drug development for rare pediatric diseases by providing additional business value. Measles is a highly contagious disease, and spreads via virus particles in bodily fluids upon close contact. Fresh Air Wild Card with Rachel Martin It's Been a Minute Machine Gods Get NPR+ More Podcasts & Shows Search Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Sign InPersonalize Your Experience Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions About NPR Diversity Support Careers Press Ethics Pennsylvania's quiet approach to measles vaccination In Pennsylvania, health officials use a quiet vaccination campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been hit hard by the measles outbreak. Special Series Only on NPR How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles November 10, 20265:00 AM ET Heard on All Things Considered Maria Godoy How word of mouth is helping an Amish community’s fight against measles Listen· 8:158-Minute ListenPlaylist Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6021511/nx-s1-9999450" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript Dale Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department. Since August, she's been leading efforts to immunize her county's Amish families against measles in their homes. Weiser poses for a portrait at the Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number. Living Better Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call. "I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes. The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care. Lower vaccination rates Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases. There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors. Animals graze at a farm in Bird-in-Hand, an agricultural community in Lancaster County, Pa., with a large Amish and Mennonite population, on Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR "They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says. But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them. "When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says. A patient, personalized approach to outreach Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says. "But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls. Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter. As with the general population, vaccine misinformation has made its way to the Amish community. And when she encounters it, Weiser takes the time to explain why the rumors are false. Chester County Public Health Director Jeanne Franklin says this kind of patient, personalized approach has helped build trust among the local Amish – who, along with conservative Mennonites, are known as the Plain community because of their simple way of life. A placard reads "work with me people" in the office of Jeanne Franklin, the public health director at the Chester County Health Department, in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR "That's why we said it has to be boots on the ground in the communities. It's not just because they were a Plain community, it was because we needed to be seen as caring people," Franklin says. Instead of relying on traditional top-down, rigid public health messaging, her staff has spent a lot of time quietly visiting Amish church leaders and businesses, introducing themselves and asking community leaders if they would hand out flyers advertising vaccine clinics. "One of them said, 'Come on back with a clinic' at his restaurant. And he helped spread the word," Franklin says. Vaccine questions and misinformation When I stopped by the restaurant, Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., an area with a sizable Amish community, I found the manager grilling chicken in an outdoor tent. Like many Amish people NPR talked to, he spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with his community's tradition of not drawing attention to oneself. A decorative sign on display near a hand washing station at Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., on Oct. 29, 2026. In August, the Amish-owned restaurant quietly hosted a vaccine clinic for the local community. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR The manager says 24 people showed up to get vaccinated at his restaurant back in August, all drawn by word of mouth. He says he decided to host the clinic for two reasons: to protect the general public and to protect his own community. He said he didn't want people blaming the Amish for spreading measles. But he says other people in the Amish community who don't regularly interact with the public aren't getting vaccinated. For some, it's because of cultural reasons, but he says others are concerned about what they've heard is in the MMR vaccine. Short Wave Vaccinated or not, we're on the brink of a measles epidemic "In my community, a lot of it has to do with what people think is in it," the manager says of the MMR vaccine. One concern he's heard repeatedly is that the vaccine contains parts of aborted fetuses. That is a myth often repeated by anti-vaccine forces, and it is one heard in conversations with Amish people in Lancaster County, home to around 45,000 Amish people. It's also the county with a third of the state's measles cases — more than 500 confirmed cases. At the Amish-owned Gordonville Book Store, where a buggy is parked outside, I meet a shopper named Lydia Esh. She says she, her husband and six adult children had all previously been vaccinated against measles. But none of her 13 grandchildren have gotten the shot, because their parents had heard that the MMR vaccine had changed and now contained aborted fetus parts — which is false. A buggy parked in the driveway at Gordonville Book Store in Gordonville, Pa., on Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR There is some evidence that anti-vaccine groups have been targeting the Amish in recent years, says Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College who has written numerous books about Amish history and culture. For example, he points to an advertisement questioning the safety of childhood vaccines published in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, an advertising publication with a large Amish readership. But in conversations around Lancaster, I also find evidence that public health outreach efforts are working. One member of the Plain community, a visibly pregnant woman outside an Amish-owned hardware store, says her husband and two children recently got vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She asked NPR not to use her name, as did an Amish man working at a produce stall in an Amish market. He says he recently got vaccinated because "measles is scary." Linda Beth Fisher, an 18-year-old Amish woman behind the counter at the Gordonville Book Store, says she is concerned that several Amish people in her area have died in the measles outbreak, but she's not sure what to believe about the MMR vaccine. Information packets are set out for patients before a Pennsylvania Department of Health MMR vaccine pop-up clinic hosted at Christiana Fire Company in Christiana, Pa., on Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR "Personally, I'm kind of leery of it. I'm not sure why," Fisher says. "I guess I've just kind of heard that they're not good, but I've also heard that they are good. So I just feel like it's two sides of the story. Would you encourage people to get it?" "They almost always come back" These types of concerns often surface at pop-up vaccine clinics like one recently hosted at the Christiana Fire Company in Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health hosts these events in Lancaster three or four times a week — all advertised by word of mouth, says Dr. Jennifer Wallace. As medical director for the department's Bureau of Community Health Systems, she oversees pop-up clinics and outreach to vulnerable communities across Pennsylvania. Bubble wands are set out for children before a Pennsylvania Department of Health MMR vaccine pop-up clinic hosted at Christiana Fire Company in Christiana, Pa., on Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR Wallace says when members of the Plain community come with questions, "We're here to give them that information and then let them ponder it. They can ask any questions they want to and then let them either get vaccinated if they choose or take that information home. Think about it. Talk with their bishops. Talk with their community. They almost always come back." Wallace says many who end up coming are families with multiple children. Tables set up around the firehouse are strewn with crayons, coloring books and bubble wands to keep young ones entertained while parents fill out paperwork. Health As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability "And then you see the kids get vaccinated and you can almost see the mother's shoulders relax over time as each child gets that shot," she says. "We've had some mothers cry afterwards because they're just so relieved." The state health department says 30 people attended the Christiana firehouse clinic, 24 of whom got vaccinated. That included a father and his three sons who arrived for their second doses. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. analysis.location_and_population: Pennsylvania, USA, Amish community.
analysis.event: A quiet vaccination campaign is being conducted by health officials to immunize Amish families against measles in their homes.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 6 confirmed measles-related deaths and over 1,500 cases (likely higher due to underreporting), with lower vaccination rates among Amish families leading to increased vulnerability to measles.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials are using a word-of-mouth approach to build trust and increase vaccination rates, with some vaccine misinformation still present.

analysis.brief_en: In Pennsylvania, health officials are using a quiet, word-of-mouth campaign to vaccinate Amish families against measles, which has caused 6 deaths and over 1,500 cases. news.content: BreakingFAA ground stop live updates: Nationwide ground stop lifted 24/7 LiveSan FranciscoEast BaySouth BayPeninsulaNorth Bay 58° Measles 8th measles-related death reported in Wisconsin: Health officials It's the first measles death in the state since 1990. ByYouri Benadjaoud Tuesday, November 10, 2026 12:37PM Watch ABC News live news stream and get 24/7 latest, breaking news coverage, and live video. An infant in Wisconsin has died from measles, the state health department said Thursday. It's the first death in the state since 1990. This brings the total number of measles deaths reported by state health departments across the country to eight: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin. Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases so far this year, the highest number in the state in more than 35 years. Nine people have required hospitalization, according to health officials. "It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family," Wisconsin Department of Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a press release. "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family." At least 96% of measles cases in the U.S. this year have been among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 degrees Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Top Stories FAA ground stop live updates: Duffy blames 'overloaded' routers; thousands of flights canceled 5 minutes ago San Francisco Bay Area Weather: Level 2 storm brings heavy rain, winds and dangerous high surf to region 1 hour ago Here's how the FAA's national ground stop is affecting Bay Area travel 2 hours ago Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek. Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says. Nationally, more than 4,800 measles cases have been confirmed this year in the U.S., with infections reported in almost every state, according to the CDC. It's the highest number of illnesses from measles since 1991. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says. Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine. AP Photo/Julio Cortez, file A second child in Grant County has died of measles, according to state health officials. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services announced the pediatric measles-associated death on Friday. No further details were released to protect the privacy of the child and their family. The news comes one week after DHS announced an infant had died of the virus, marking the first measles death in the state since 1990. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Instagram This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email Measles is one of the most contagious viruses, and it can cause life-threatening complications including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. Children younger than age 5 are among those who are most at risk of serious illness, as well as people who are pregnant or who have weakened immune systems. Wisconsin health officials advise early measles vaccination for some infants amid outbreak Doctors recommend children receive the first dose of the two-shot measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine after their first birthday. But DHS announced last week that it recommends children as young as 6 months who are at increased risk of exposure to measles get the shot. The two-dose course of the MMR vaccine is 97 percent effective at preventing measles and provides lifelong protection. As of Friday, there have been 651 measles cases reported across 22 Wisconsin counties this year. It’s the highest number of cases in the state in more than 35 years, according to DHS, and likely does not reflect the full extent of spread due to underreporting. Speaking to PBS Wisconsin’s Here & Now, Dr. Ryan Westergaard, chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases at DHS, said it’s safe to assume the state has “well over 1,000 cases.” “When we investigate cases in the community, we hear about families saying that there are other families that we don’t know about,” he said. “We know that with all of our conditions that are reportable to public health, they don’t all get reported. Some people don’t get tested, some people don’t come to medical attention.” Westergaard pointed out that in the decade before the COVID-19 pandemic, Wisconsin saw between zero and two cases of measles most years. But he said the unchecked spread of the virus this year is not surprising given the state’s low childhood vaccination rates. “This is really something that we haven’t seen in our careers, and we fear we’re not quite through it,” he said. “It’s likely to continue to get worse.” Wisconsin has the fourth-highest number of measles cases in the U.S. this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania, which has the most measles cases for the year, reported the state’s seventh-measles related death on Friday. New York health officials reported Monday that a child had died of the virus, marking that state’s first measles death in more than 30 years. Listen · 9:35 min Share full article A towering pile of logs attested to work unfinished amid a measles outbreak in Lewis County, N.Y.Credit...David Andreatta By Joseph Goldstein and David Andreatta Joseph Goldstein reported from New York City, and David Andreatta from Lewis County, N.Y., where an infant died from measles. Nov. 11, 2026 On a recent Saturday morning in New York’s North Country, there were signs that work had fallen behind. Standing on his porch in suspenders and shirtsleeves, 32-year-old David Stoltzfus pointed at a heap of logs, some thicker than telephone poles and stacked two stories high. He needed to saw them into lumber. But Mr. Stoltzfus was still playing catch-up after falling ill. “You see the big pile of wood that all got piled up?” he asked, pointing to hundreds of logs. “That’s because of the measles.” Subscribe to The Times to read as many articles as you like.
